- Year 3: 300 units, cost 300, profit 210, tax 15%: [latex]0.85\,SP=510\Rightarrow SP=600[/latex]

Ratio = 800 : 600 = 4 : 3

Answer: 4 : 3

questions.subject: General Aptitude
questions.text:
Six students P, Q, R, S, T and U, with distinct heights, compare their heights and make the following observations.

Observation I: S is taller than R.
Observation II: Q is the shortest of all.
Observation III: U is taller than only one student.
Observation IV: T is taller than S but is not the tallest

The number of students that are taller than R is the same as the number of students shorter than ____________.
questions.solution:
From the observations: Q is shortest, U is second shortest, and T is taller than S but not tallest, so P is the tallest. R is shorter than S and above U.

Order (short [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] tall): Q, U, R, S, T, P.

Taller than R: S, T, P = 3. Shorter than S: R, U, Q = 3.

Answer: S

questions.subject: Algorithm
questions.text: Which one of the following statements is TRUE for all positive functions [latex]f(n)[/latex]?
questions.solution:
Checking each option:
- Polynomial [latex]f(n)=n^k[/latex]: [latex]f(n^2)=n^{2k}[/latex] and [latex]f(n)^2=n^{2k}[/latex], so [latex]f(n^2)=\Theta(f(n)^2)[/latex] [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE.
- [latex]f(n^2)=o(f(n)^2)[/latex] fails for polynomials (they are equal, not strictly smaller).
- For [latex]f(n)=2^n[/latex]: [latex]f(n^2)=2^{n^2}[/latex] but [latex]f(n)^2=2^{2n}[/latex]; [latex]2^{n^2}[/latex] grows much faster, so [latex]O[/latex] fails.
- For [latex]f(n)=2^{-n}[/latex]: [latex]f(n^2)=2^{-n^2}[/latex] is much smaller than [latex]f(n)^2=2^{-2n}[/latex], so [latex]\Omega[/latex] fails.

Answer: [latex]f(n^2)=\Theta(f(n)^2)[/latex], where f(n) is a polynomial

questions.subject: Theory of Computation
questions.text: Which one of the following regular expressions correctly represents the language of the finite automaton given below?
questions.solution:
The start state is not final. From start:
- on a go to the upper final state (loops on b, returns to start on b) [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] one round trip is [latex]ab^*b[/latex];
- on b go to the lower final state (loops on a, returns to start on a) [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] one round trip is [latex]ba^*a[/latex].

So: any number of round trips [latex](ab^*b+ba^*a)^*[/latex], and then finish in one of the final states: [latex]ab^*[/latex] or [latex]ba^*[/latex].

Answer: [latex](ba^*a+ab^*b)^*(ab^*+ba^*)[/latex]

questions.subject: Compiler Design
questions.text: Which one of the following statements is TRUE?
options:
The LALR(1) parser for a grammar G cannot have reduce-reduce conflict if the
LR(1) parser for G does not have reduce-reduce conflict.
Symbol table is accessed only during the lexical analysis phase.
Data flow analysis is necessary for run-time memory management.
LR(1) parsing is sufficient for deterministic context-free languages.
questions.solution:
Checking each statement:
- LALR(1) merges LR(1) states with the same core; this merging can create a new reduce-reduce conflict [latex]\text{---}[/latex] FALSE.
- The symbol table is used in almost every phase (semantic analysis, code generation, [latex]\ldots[/latex]) [latex]\text{---}[/latex] FALSE.
- Data flow analysis is used for code optimization, not run-time memory management [latex]\text{---}[/latex] FALSE.
- Every deterministic CFL has an LR(1) grammar, so LR(1) parsing is sufficient for DCFLs [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE.

Answer: LR(1) parsing is sufficient for deterministic context-free languages

questions.subject: Database Management System
questions.text: In a relational data model, which one of the following statements is TRUE?
options: A relation with only two attributes is always in BCNF.
If all attributes of a relation are prime attributes, then the relation is in BCNF.
Every relation has at least one non-prime attribute.
questions.solution:
Checking each statement:
- Relation R(A, B): the only possible non-trivial FDs are [latex]A\rightarrow B[/latex] or [latex]B\rightarrow A[/latex]. In each case the left side is a key, so R is always in BCNF [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE.
- All attributes prime guarantees 3NF, not BCNF (e.g. [latex]AB\rightarrow C,\ C\rightarrow B[/latex]) [latex]\text{---}[/latex] FALSE.
- A relation can have no non-prime attribute (e.g. all attributes form the key) [latex]\text{---}[/latex] FALSE.
- BCNF decomposition does not always preserve FDs [latex]\text{---}[/latex] FALSE.

Answer: A relation with only two attributes is always in BCNF

questions.subject: Data Structure
questions.text:
Consider the problem of reversing a singly linked list. To take an example, given the linked list below,

the reversed linked list should look like

Which one of the following statements is TRUE about the time complexity of algorithms that solve the above problem in O(1) space?
options: The best algorithm for the problem takes [latex]\theta(n)[/latex] time in the worst case.
The best algorithm for the problem takes [latex]\theta(n \log n)[/latex] time in the worst case.
The best algorithm for the problem takes [latex]\theta(n^2)[/latex] time in the worst case.
It is not possible to reverse a singly linked list in O(1) space.
questions.solution:
Walk the list once with three pointers (prev, curr, next), reversing each link as you go:
next = curr[latex]\rightarrow[/latex]next; curr[latex]\rightarrow[/latex]next = prev; prev = curr; curr = next.

Each node is visited once and only 3 extra pointers are used, so it takes [latex]\Theta(n)[/latex] time in [latex]O(1)[/latex] space. It cannot be faster, because every link must be changed.

Answer: The best algorithm takes [latex]\theta(n)[/latex] time in the worst case

questions.subject: Data Structure
questions.text:
Suppose we are given [latex]n[/latex] keys, [latex]m[/latex] hash table slots, and two simple uniform hash functions [latex]h_1[/latex] and [latex]h_2[/latex]. Further suppose our hashing scheme uses [latex]h_1[/latex] for the odd keys
and [latex]h_2[/latex] for the even keys. What is the expected number of keys in a slot?
questions.solution:
Both [latex]h_1[/latex] and [latex]h_2[/latex] are simple uniform hash functions, so every key (odd or even) lands in any given slot with probability [latex]\frac{1}{m}[/latex].

Expected keys in a slot [latex]=n\times\frac{1}{m}=\frac{n}{m}[/latex] (which hash function is used does not matter).

Answer: [latex]\frac{n}{m}[/latex]

questions.subject: Computer Organization
questions.text: Which one of the following facilitates transfer of bulk data from hard disk to main memory with the highest throughput?
questions.solution:
In DMA, the DMA controller moves the whole block between disk and memory directly, without the CPU handling every word. Interrupt-driven, polling and programmed I/O all need the CPU for each word, so they are much slower for bulk data.

Answer: DMA based I/O transfer

questions.subject: Digital Logic
questions.text: Let R1 and R2 be two 4-bit registers that store numbers in 2's complement form. For the operation R1+R2, which one of the following values of R1 and R2 gives an arithmetic overflow?
questions.solution:
4-bit 2's complement range: [latex]-8[/latex] to [latex]+7[/latex].

- 1011 + 1110 = [latex](-5)+(-2)=-7[/latex] [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] fits
- 1100 + 1010 = [latex](-4)+(-6)=-10[/latex] [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] overflow
- 0011 + 0100 = [latex]3+4=7[/latex] [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] fits
- 1001 + 1111 = [latex](-7)+(-1)=-8[/latex] [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] fits

Answer: R1 = 1100 and R2 = 1010

questions.subject: Operating System
questions.text:
Consider the following threads, [latex]T_1, T_2, \text{ and }T_3[/latex] executing on a single processor, synchronized using three binary semaphore variables, [latex]S_1, S_2, \text{ and }S_3[/latex], operated upon using standard [latex]wait()[/latex] and [latex]signal()[/latex]. The threads can be context switched in any order and at any time.

Which initialization of the semaphores would print the sequence BCABCABCA ...?
questions.solution:
From the code: T2 prints B (needs [latex]S_1[/latex], then signals [latex]S_3[/latex]), T1 prints C (needs [latex]S_3[/latex], signals [latex]S_2[/latex]), T3 prints A (needs [latex]S_2[/latex], signals [latex]S_1[/latex]).

The output must start with B, so only T2 may run first: [latex]S_1=1[/latex] and [latex]S_2=S_3=0[/latex]. Then the chain B [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] C [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] A [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] B [latex]\ldots[/latex] repeats forever.

(If [latex]S_2[/latex] or [latex]S_3[/latex] were 1, A or C could be printed first.)

Answer: [latex]S_1=1;\ S_2=0;\ S_3=0[/latex]

questions.subject: Engineering Mathematics
questions.text:
Consider the following two statements with respect to the matrices [latex]A_{m \times n},B_{n \times m},C_{n \times n} \text{ and }D_{n \times n},[/latex]

Statement 1: [latex]tr(AB) = tr(BA)[/latex]
Statement 2: [latex]tr(CD) = tr(DC)[/latex]

where[latex]tr()[/latex] represents the trace of a matrix. Which one of the following holds?
options: Statement 1 is correct and Statement 2 is wrong.
Statement 1 is wrong and Statement 2 is correct.
Both Statement 1 and Statement 2 are correct.
Both Statement 1 and Statement 2 are wrong.
questions.solution:
[latex]tr(AB)=\sum_i\sum_k a_{ik}b_{ki}=\sum_k\sum_i b_{ki}a_{ik}=tr(BA)[/latex]. This holds for any [latex]A_{m\times n}[/latex], [latex]B_{n\times m}[/latex] (AB is [latex]m\times m[/latex], BA is [latex]n\times n[/latex]).

Statement 2 is the special case of square matrices, so it is also true.

Answer: Both Statement 1 and Statement 2 are correct

questions.subject: C Programming
questions.solution:
Trace the program line by line:
- p = [latex]\&[/latex]x; *p = 10 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] x = 10
- p = [latex]\&[/latex]z[1] (not used afterwards)
- [latex]*(\&z[0]+1)[/latex] is z[1], so z[1] += 3 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] z[1] = 14
- z[0] is unchanged [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] 10

Output: 10, 10, 14

Answer: 10, 10, 14

questions.subject: Computer Network
questions.text:
Consider an enterprise network with two Ethernet segments, a web server and a firewall, connected via three routers as shown below.

What is the number of subnets inside the enterprise network?
questions.solution:
Every link between router interfaces (and every LAN behind a router) is a separate subnet:
1. Firewall - left router
2. Firewall - top router
3. Top router - web server
4. Top router - right router
5. Left router - left Ethernet
6. Right router - right Ethernet

Answer: 6

questions.subject: Theory of Computation
questions.text: Which of the following statements is/are TRUE?
options: Every subset of a recursively enumerable language is recursive.
If a language [latex]L[/latex] and its complement [latex]\bar{L}[/latex] are both recursively enumerable, then [latex]L[/latex] must be recursive.
Complement of a context-free language must be recursive.
If [latex]L_1[/latex] and [latex]L_2[/latex] are regular, then [latex]L_1 \cap L_2 [/latex]must be deterministic context-free.
questions.solution:
Checking each statement:
- A subset of an RE language need not be recursive (e.g. the halting language is a subset of [latex]\Sigma^*[/latex]) [latex]\text{---}[/latex] FALSE.
- If [latex]L[/latex] and [latex]\bar L[/latex] are both RE, run both recognizers in parallel; one must accept, so [latex]L[/latex] is recursive [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE.
- Every CFL is recursive and recursive languages are closed under complement [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE.
- [latex]L_1\cap L_2[/latex] is regular, and every regular language is deterministic context-free [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE.

Answer: Options 2, 3 and 4

questions.subject: Computer Organization
questions.text: Let WB and WT be two set associative cache organizations that use LRU algorithm for cache block replacement. WB is a write back cache and WT is a write through cache. Which of the following statements is/are FALSE?
options: Each cache block in WB and WT has a dirty bit.
Every write hit in WB leads to a data transfer from cache to main memory.
Eviction of a block from WT will not lead to data transfer from cache to main memory.
A read miss in WB will never lead to eviction of a dirty block from WB.
questions.solution:
Check each statement (we need the FALSE ones):
- "Each block in WB and WT has a dirty bit": WT writes memory on every write, so it needs no dirty bit [latex]\text{---}[/latex] FALSE.
- "Every write hit in WB transfers data to memory": WB only sets the dirty bit; memory is updated on eviction [latex]\text{---}[/latex] FALSE.
- "Eviction from WT causes no transfer to memory": memory is already up to date [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE.
- "A read miss in WB never evicts a dirty block": the LRU victim can be dirty [latex]\text{---}[/latex] FALSE.

Answer: Options 1, 2 and 4

questions.subject: Database Management System
questions.text:
Consider the following three relations in a relational database.
[latex]Employee(eId, Name), Brand (bId, bName), Own(eId ,bId)[/latex]
Which of the following relational algebra expressions return the set of [latex]eIds[/latex] who own all the brands?
questions.solution:
"Owns all brands" is relational division by the set of all brands.

- Option 1: [latex]\Pi_{eId,bId}(Own)\div\Pi_{bId}(Brand)[/latex] [latex]\text{---}[/latex] exactly division [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE.
- Option 2: [latex]\Pi_{eId}(Own)\times\Pi_{bId}(Brand)[/latex] lists every (employee, brand) pair; subtracting Own leaves the pairs an employee does not own. Removing those employees leaves those who own every brand [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE (this is the expansion of division).
- Option 3 divides by [latex]\Pi_{bId}(Own)[/latex] (brands owned by someone); a brand owned by nobody would be ignored [latex]\text{---}[/latex] wrong.
- Option 4 divides a full cross product, which returns every employee [latex]\text{---}[/latex] wrong.

Answer: Options 1 and 2

questions.subject: Operating System
questions.text: Which of the following statements is/are TRUE with respect to deadlocks?
options: Circular wait is a necessary condition for the formation of deadlock.
In a system where each resource has more than one instance, a cycle in its wait-for graph indicates the presence of a deadlock.
If the current allocation of resources to processes leads the system to unsafe state, then deadlock will necessarily occur.
In the resource-allocation graph of a system, if every edge is an assignment edge, then the system is not in deadlock state.
questions.solution:
Checking each statement:
- Circular wait is one of the four necessary conditions (with mutual exclusion, hold [latex]\&[/latex] wait, no preemption) [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE.
- With multiple instances per resource, a cycle is necessary but not sufficient for deadlock [latex]\text{---}[/latex] FALSE.
- An unsafe state only may lead to deadlock; processes might release resources early [latex]\text{---}[/latex] FALSE.
- If every edge is an assignment edge, no process is waiting for anything, so there is no deadlock [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE.

Answer: Options 1 and 4

questions.subject: Discrete Mathematics
questions.text: Which of the following statements is/are TRUE for a group [latex]G[/latex]?
options: If for all [latex]x,y \in G, (xy)^2=x^2y^2[/latex], then [latex]G[/latex] is commutative.
If for all [latex]x \in G, x^2=1[/latex], then [latex]G[/latex] is commutative. Here, 1 is the identity element of [latex]G[/latex].
If the order of [latex]G[/latex] is 2 , then [latex]G[/latex] is commutative.
If [latex]G[/latex] is commutative, then a subgroup of [latex]G[/latex] need not be commutative.
questions.solution:
Checking each statement:
- [latex](xy)^2=x^2y^2[/latex] means [latex]xyxy=xxyy[/latex]. Cancel x on the left and y on the right: [latex]yx=xy[/latex] [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE.
- [latex]x^2=1[/latex] means every element is its own inverse. Then [latex]xy=(xy)^{-1}=y^{-1}x^{-1}=yx[/latex] [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE.
- A group of order 2 is [latex]\{1,a\}[/latex], which is cyclic, hence commutative [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE.
- Every subgroup of a commutative group is commutative (same operation) [latex]\text{---}[/latex] FALSE.

Answer: Options 1, 2 and 3

questions.subject: Data Structure
questions.text: Suppose a binary search tree with 1000 distinct elements is also a complete binary tree. The tree is stored using the array representation of binary heap trees. Assuming that the array indices start with 0, the 3rd largest element of the tree is stored at index _______.
questions.solution:
Complete tree with 1000 nodes (indices 0-999). Children of i: [latex]2i+1[/latex], [latex]2i+2[/latex].

- Largest = go right as far as possible: 0 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] 2 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] 6 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] 14 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] 30 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] 62 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] 126 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] 254 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] 510. Its children 1021, 1022 do not exist, so index 510 is the largest.
- 2nd largest = predecessor of 510. It has no left child, so it is its parent: index 254.
- 3rd largest = maximum of the left subtree of 254. Left child = 509; its children 1019, 1020 do not exist, so it is 509.

Answer: 509

questions.subject: Compiler Design
questions.text:
Consider the augmented grammar with [latex] \{+, *, (, ), id \}[/latex] as the set of terminals.
[latex] \begin{aligned}&S' \rightarrow S \\ &S \rightarrow S+R|R \\ &R \rightarrow R*P|P \\ &P \rightarrow (S)|id \end{aligned}[/latex]
If [latex]I_0[/latex] is the set of two [latex]LR(0)[/latex] items [latex] \{ [S' \rightarrow S.], [S \rightarrow S.+R] \}[/latex], then [latex]goto(closure(I_0 ),+)[/latex] contains exactly ______ items.
questions.solution:
Closure of [latex]I_0[/latex] adds nothing (the dot is before + and at the end, not before a non-terminal).

goto on +: [latex]S\rightarrow S+.R[/latex]. Closure (dot before R, then before P):
1. [latex]S\rightarrow S+.R[/latex]
2. [latex]R\rightarrow .R*P[/latex]
3. [latex]R\rightarrow .P[/latex]
4. [latex]P\rightarrow .(S)[/latex]
5. [latex]P\rightarrow .id[/latex]

Answer: 5

questions.subject: Discrete Mathematics
questions.text: Consider a simple undirected graph of 10 vertices. If the graph is disconnected, then the maximum number of edges it can have is .
questions.solution:
A disconnected graph has at least two components. To keep as many edges as possible, make one component [latex]K_9[/latex] and leave 1 vertex isolated.

Edges [latex]=\binom{9}{2}=36[/latex] (in general [latex]\binom{n-1}{2}[/latex]).

Answer: 36

questions.subject: Database Management System
questions.text:
Consider a relation [latex]R( A, B, C, D, E )[/latex] with the following three functional dependencies.
[latex]AB \rightarrow C;BC \rightarrow D; C \rightarrow E;[/latex]
The number of superkeys in the relation [latex]R[/latex] is .
questions.solution:
A and B never appear on the right side of any FD, so every key must contain A and B.
[latex]AB^+=AB\rightarrow ABC\rightarrow ABCD\rightarrow ABCDE[/latex], so AB is the only candidate key.

Superkeys = AB plus any subset of {C, D, E}: [latex]2^3=8[/latex].

Answer: 8

questions.subject: Discrete Mathematics
questions.text: The number of arrangements of six identical balls in three identical bins is ____.
questions.solution:
Balls and bins are both identical, so we count partitions of 6 into at most 3 parts:
6, 5+1, 4+2, 3+3, 4+1+1, 3+2+1, 2+2+2

Answer: 7

questions.subject: Computer Organization
questions.text: A cache memory that has a hit rate of 0.8 has an access latency 10 ns and miss penalty 100 ns. An optimization is done on the cache to reduce the miss rate. However, the optimization results in an increase of cache access latency to 15 ns, whereas the miss penalty is not affected. The minimum hit rate (rounded off to two decimal places) needed after the optimization such that it should not increase the average memory access time is _____.
questions.solution:
Average memory access time = hit latency + miss rate [latex]\times[/latex] miss penalty.

Before: [latex]10+0.2\times100=30[/latex] ns.
After: [latex]15+(1-h)\times100\le30\Rightarrow1-h\le0.15\Rightarrow h\ge0.85[/latex]

Answer: 0.85

questions.subject: Engineering Mathematics
questions.text:
The value of the following limit is _____
[latex] \lim_{x \to 0+} \frac{ \sqrt{x}}{1-e^{2 \sqrt{x}}}[/latex]
questions.solution:
Let [latex]t=\sqrt x\to0^+[/latex]: the limit is [latex]\lim_{t\to0}\frac{t}{1-e^{2t}}[/latex] (form 0/0).

Since [latex]e^{2t}\approx1+2t[/latex]: [latex]\frac{t}{1-e^{2t}}\approx\frac{t}{-2t}=-\frac12[/latex] (same by L'Hospital: [latex]\frac{1}{-2e^{2t}}\to-\frac12[/latex]).

Answer: -0.5

questions.subject: Computer Network
questions.text: Consider the resolution of the domain name [latex]www.gate.org.in[/latex] by a DNS resolver. Assume that no resource records are cached anywhere across the DNS servers and that iterative query mechanism is used in the resolution. The number of DNS query-response pairs involved in completely resolving the domain name is .
questions.solution:
With iterative resolution and empty caches, the resolver asks each level in turn:
1. Root server [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] refers to the .in server
2. .in server [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] refers to org.in
3. org.in server [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] refers to gate.org.in
4. gate.org.in server [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] returns the IP of www.gate.org.in

Answer: 4

questions.subject: Discrete Mathematics
questions.solution:
Write [latex]a_n=1+b_n[/latex], where [latex]b_n=n[/latex] for odd n and 0 otherwise.

- [latex]\sum x^n=\frac{1}{1-x}[/latex]
- [latex]\sum_{n\text{ odd}}x^n=\frac{x}{1-x^2}[/latex], so [latex]\sum_{n\text{ odd}}nx^n=x\frac{d}{dx}\left(\frac{x}{1-x^2}\right)=x\cdot\frac{1+x^2}{(1-x^2)^2}[/latex]

[latex]G(x)=\frac{x(1+x^2)}{(1-x^2)^2}+\frac{1}{1-x}[/latex]

Answer: Option 1

questions.subject: Discrete Mathematics
questions.text: Consider a simple undirected unweighted graph with at least three vertices. If [latex]A[/latex] is the adjacency matrix of the graph, then the number of 3-cycles in the graph is given by the trace of
questions.solution:
[latex](A^3)_{ii}[/latex] = number of closed walks of length 3 starting at vertex i, i.e. triangles through i, each counted twice (two directions).

In the trace, every triangle appears at each of its 3 vertices [latex]\times[/latex] 2 directions = 6 times.

Number of triangles [latex]=\frac{tr(A^3)}{6}[/latex]

Answer: [latex]A^3[/latex] divided by 6

questions.subject: Operating System
questions.text: Which one of the following statements is FALSE?
options: The TLB performs an associative search in parallel on all its valid entries using page number of incoming virtual address.
If the virtual address of a word given by CPU has a TLB hit, but the subsequent search for the word results in a cache miss, then the word will always be present in the main memory.
The memory access time using a given inverted page table is always same for all incoming virtual addresses.
In a system that uses hashed page tables, if two distinct virtual addresses V1 and V2 map to the same value while hashing, then the memory access time of these addresses will not be the same.
questions.solution:
Check each statement (we need the FALSE one):
- The TLB is associative memory and compares all entries in parallel [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE.
- A TLB hit means the page is in main memory, so on a cache miss the word is surely in main memory [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE.
- Inverted page table: the frame is found by searching (or hashing and following a chain), so the time depends on the address [latex]\text{---}[/latex] FALSE.
- In a hashed page table, colliding addresses sit on the same chain at different positions, so their access times differ [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE.

Answer: Option 3 is FALSE

questions.subject: Database Management System
questions.text:
Let [latex]R_i(z)[/latex] and [latex]W_i(z)[/latex] denote read and write operations on a data element [latex]z[/latex] by a transaction [latex]T_i[/latex], respectively. Consider the schedule [latex]S[/latex] with four transactions.

S: [latex]R_4(x)R_2(x)R_3(x)R_1(y)W_1(y)W_2 (x)W_3 (y)R_4(y)[/latex]

Which one of the following serial schedules is conflict equivalent to [latex]S[/latex]?
questions.solution:
Conflicting pairs in S:
- [latex]R_4(x)[/latex] before [latex]W_2(x)[/latex]: T4 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] T2
- [latex]R_3(x)[/latex] before [latex]W_2(x)[/latex]: T3 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] T2
- [latex]R_1(y)/W_1(y)[/latex] before [latex]W_3(y)[/latex]: T1 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] T3
- [latex]W_1(y)[/latex] before [latex]R_4(y)[/latex]: T1 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] T4
- [latex]W_3(y)[/latex] before [latex]R_4(y)[/latex]: T3 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] T4

Topological order: T1 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] T3 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] T4 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] T2.

Answer: [latex]T_1\rightarrow T_3\rightarrow T_4\rightarrow T_2[/latex]

questions.subject: Computer Organization
questions.topic: ALU Data Path and Control Unit
questions.text: Consider a digital display system (DDS) shown in the figure that displays the contents of register X. A 16-bit code word is used to load a word in X, either from S or from R. S is a 1024-word memory segment and R is a 32-word register file. Based on the value of mode bit M, T selects an input word to load in X. P and Q interface with the corresponding bits in the code word to choose the addressed word. Which one of the following represents the functionality of P, Q, and T?
options:
P is 10:1 multiplexer;
Q is 5:1 multiplexer;
T is 2:1 multiplexer

P is [latex]10:2^{10}[/latex] decoder;
Q is [latex]5:2^{5}[/latex] decoder;
T is 2:1 encoder

P is [latex]10:2^{10}[/latex] decoder;
Q is [latex]5:2^{5}[/latex] decoder;
T is 2:1 multiplexer

P is 1:10 de-multiplexer;
Q is 1:5 de-multiplexer;
T is 2:1 multiplexer
questions.solution:
Match each block with its job:
- S has 1024 words, so the S-address is 10 bits. P must activate exactly one of 1024 words [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] 10 : [latex]2^{10}[/latex] decoder.
- R has 32 words, so the R-address is 5 bits [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] Q is a 5 : [latex]2^5[/latex] decoder.
- T chooses one of two inputs (from S or R) using mode bit M [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] 2 : 1 multiplexer.

Answer: P is 10:2^10 decoder; Q is 5:2^5 decoder; T is 2:1 multiplexer

questions.subject: Digital Logic
questions.text:
Consider three floating point numbers A, B and C stored in registers [latex]R_A[/latex], [latex]R_B[/latex] and [latex]R_C[/latex], respectively as per IEEE-754 single precision floating point format. The 32-bit content stored in these registers (in hexadecimal form) are as follows.

[latex]R_A=0xC1400000[/latex]
[latex]R_B=0x42100000[/latex]
[latex]R_C=0x41400000[/latex]

Which one of the following is FALSE?
questions.solution:
Decode each number (sign | exponent | mantissa):
- [latex]R_A=[/latex] C1400000: sign 1, exponent [latex]130\Rightarrow2^3[/latex], mantissa 1.1[latex]{}_2[/latex] = 1.5 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] [latex]A=-12[/latex]
- [latex]R_B=[/latex] 42100000: sign 0, exponent [latex]132\Rightarrow2^5[/latex], mantissa 1.001[latex]{}_2[/latex] = 1.125 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] [latex]B=36[/latex]
- [latex]R_C=[/latex] 41400000: same as A but positive [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] [latex]C=12[/latex]

- [latex]A+C=0[/latex] True
- [latex]A+B=24\ne12=C[/latex] [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] FALSE
- [latex]B=36=3C[/latex] True
- [latex]B-C=24 \gt 0[/latex] True

Answer: C = A + B

questions.subject: Operating System
questions.text: Consider four processes P, Q, R, and S scheduled on a CPU as per round robin algorithm with a time quantum of 4 units. The processes arrive in the order P, Q, R, S, all at time t = 0. There is exactly one context switch from S to Q, exactly one context switch from R to Q, and exactly two context switches from Q to R. There is no context switch from S to P. Switching to a ready process after the termination of another process is also considered a context switch. Which one of the following is NOT possible as CPU burst time (in time units) of these processes?
questions.solution:
Simulate round robin (quantum 4, order P, Q, R, S) for option 4: P = 3, Q = 7, R = 7, S = 3.
- P runs 3 and finishes [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] Q runs 4 (3 left) [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] R runs 4 (3 left) [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] S runs 3 and finishes
- [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] Q runs 3 and finishes [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] R runs 3 and finishes

Switches: P[latex]\rightarrow[/latex]Q, Q[latex]\rightarrow[/latex]R, R[latex]\rightarrow[/latex]S, S[latex]\rightarrow[/latex]Q, Q[latex]\rightarrow[/latex]R. There is no R [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] Q switch, but exactly one is required. So these burst times are impossible.

(Simulating the other three options gives exactly one S[latex]\rightarrow[/latex]Q, one R[latex]\rightarrow[/latex]Q, two Q[latex]\rightarrow[/latex]R and no S[latex]\rightarrow[/latex]P.)

Answer: P = 3, Q = 7, R = 7, S = 3

questions.subject: C Programming
questions.solution:
Each inner brace gives 9 values to [latex]a[i][\,][\,][/latex], filled row by row:
a[0][0] = {1, 2, 3}, a[1][0] = {10, 11, 12}, a[2][0] = {19, 20, 21}, [latex]\ldots[/latex]

j stays 0, and the loops print [latex]a[i][0][k][/latex] for k = 0, 1, 2:
1 2 3
10 11 12
19 20 21

Answer: 1 2 3 / 10 11 12 / 19 20 21

questions.subject: C Programming
Engineering Mathematics
questions.solution:
Using Doolittle LU (unit diagonal in L):
- Row 1 of U = [1, 1, [latex]-[/latex]2]; [latex]L_{21}=1,\ L_{31}=2[/latex]
- [latex]U_{22}=3-1=2,\ U_{23}=-1-(-2)=1[/latex]
- [latex]L_{32}=\frac{1-2\cdot1}{2}=-\frac12[/latex]
- [latex]U_{33}=-5-2(-2)-(-\frac12)(1)=-\frac12[/latex]

Solving the system: eq2 [latex]-[/latex] eq1 gives [latex]2x_2+x_3=3[/latex]; eq3 [latex]-[/latex] 2[latex]\cdot[/latex]eq1 gives [latex]x_2+x_3=1[/latex]. So [latex]x_2=2,\ x_3=-1,\ x_1=4-2-2=0[/latex].

Answer: [latex]L_{32}=-\frac12,\ U_{33}=-\frac12,\ x_1=0[/latex]

questions.subject: Theory of Computation
questions.text: Which of the following is/are undecidable?
options: Given two Turing machines M1 and M2 , decide if L(M1 ) = L(M2 ).
Given a Turing machine M , decide if L(M ) is regular.
Given a Turing machine M , decide if M accepts all strings.
Given a Turing machine M , decide if M takes more than 1073 steps on every string.
questions.solution:
Options 1-3 ask about a non-trivial property of the language of a TM (equality, regularity, accepting everything). By Rice's theorem they are undecidable.

Option 4 is decidable: in 1073 steps a TM can read at most the first 1073 input symbols, so it is enough to simulate M for 1073 steps on the finitely many strings of length up to 1073.

Answer: Options 1, 2 and 3

questions.subject: Theory of Computation
options: [latex]L_1[/latex] and [latex]L_2[/latex]  are context-free but not regular.
questions.solution:
Look at each language closely:
- [latex]L_1[/latex]: n can be 0, so taking n = 0, [latex]L_1=\{w\}=(a+b)^*[/latex] [latex]\text{---}[/latex] regular.
- [latex]L_2[/latex]: [latex]|w|\ge1[/latex] and x can be anything, so it is enough that the string starts and ends with the same symbol with something in between: [latex]a(a+b)^+a+b(a+b)^+b[/latex] [latex]\text{---}[/latex] regular.

Both are regular, hence also context-free. So options 1, 2 and 3 are true; "context-free but not regular" is false.

Answer: Options 1, 2 and 3

questions.subject: Theory of Computation
options: [latex]L_1[/latex] is not context-free but [latex]L_2[/latex] and [latex]L_3[/latex] are deterministic context-free.
Neither [latex]L_1[/latex] nor its complement is context-free.
questions.solution:
Facts: [latex]L_1=\{ww\}[/latex] is not CFL but its complement is CFL. [latex]L_2=a^nb^nc^m[/latex] and [latex]L_3=a^mb^nc^n[/latex] are DCFLs.

- Option 1: true.
- Option 2: [latex]L_2[/latex] is context-free [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] statement FALSE.
- Option 3: [latex]L_2\cap L_3=\{a^nb^nc^n\}[/latex] is not context-free [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] FALSE.
- Option 4: the complement of [latex]L_1[/latex] is context-free [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] FALSE.

Answer: Options 2, 3 and 4

questions.subject: Algorithm
questions.text: Consider a simple undirected weighted graph G, all of whose edge weights are distinct. Which of the following statements about the minimum spanning trees of G is/are TRUE?
options: The edge with the second smallest weight is always part of any minimum spanning tree of G .
One or both of the edges with the third smallest and the fourth smallest weights are part of any minimum spanning tree of G .

Suppose [latex]S\subseteq V[/latex] be such that [latex]S\neq  \phi [/latex] and [latex]S\neq  V[/latex] . Consider the edge with the minimum weight such that one of its vertices is in S and the other in V \ S . Such an edge will always be part of any minimum spanning tree of G .
G can have multiple minimum spanning trees.
questions.solution:
With distinct weights the MST is unique (so option 4 is false).

- The two smallest edges cannot form a cycle, so Kruskal always takes both [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE.
- If the 3rd smallest is rejected, it closes a triangle with the two smallest edges. Then the 4th edge cannot form a cycle with them (the triangle's 3 vertices are already fully joined), so it is taken [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE.
- This is the cut property: the lightest edge crossing any cut is in every MST [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE.

Answer: Options 1, 2 and 3

questions.subject: Discrete Mathematics
questions.text:
The following simple undirected graph is referred to as the Peterson graph.

Which of the following statements is/are TRUE?
options: The chromatic number of the graph is 3.
The graph has a Hamiltonian path.
The following graph is isomorphic to the Peterson graph.
The size of the largest independent set of the given graph is 3. (A subset of vertices of a graph form an independent set if no two vertices of the subset are adjacent.)
questions.solution:
Petersen graph: 10 vertices, 3-regular, no triangles or 4-cycles.

- Odd cycles (5-cycles) need 3 colours, and 3 are enough [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] chromatic number 3 [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE.
- It has no Hamiltonian cycle, but it does have a Hamiltonian path (outer cycle 4 vertices, then into the star) [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE.
- The given graph is also 3-regular on 10 vertices with girth 5, and is a known drawing of the Petersen graph [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE.
- The largest independent set has size 4, not 3 [latex]\text{---}[/latex] FALSE.

Answer: Options 1, 2 and 3

questions.subject: Discrete Mathematics
questions.text:
Consider the following recurrence:
[latex] \begin{aligned} f(1)&=1; \\ f(2n)&=2f(n)-1, & \text{for }n \geq 1; \\ f(2n+1)&=2f(n)+1, & \text{for }n \geq 1. \end{aligned}[/latex]
Then, which of the following statements is/are TRUE?
questions.solution:
Compute some values: f(1)=1, f(2)=1, f(3)=3, f(4)=1, f(5)=3, f(6)=5, f(7)=7, f(8)=1, f(10)=5, f(20)=9.

- [latex]f(2^n-1)=2^n-1[/latex]: f(1)=1, f(3)=3, f(7)=7 True (by induction [latex]f(2m+1)=2f(m)+1[/latex])
- [latex]f(2^n)=1[/latex]: [latex]f(2^n)=2f(2^{n-1})-1=2-1=1[/latex] True
- [latex]f(5\cdot2^n)=2^{n+1}+1[/latex]: f(5)=3, f(10)=5, f(20)=9 True
- [latex]f(2^n+1)=2^n+1[/latex]: f(5)=3 [latex]\ne[/latex] 5 False

Answer: Options 1, 2 and 3

questions.subject: Discrete Mathematics
questions.text: Which of the properties hold for the adjacency matrix [latex]A[/latex] of a simple undirected unweighted graph having [latex]n[/latex] vertices?
options: The diagonal entries of [latex]A^2[/latex] are the degrees of the vertices of the graph.
If the graph is connected, then none of the entries of [latex]A^{n-1}+I_n[/latex]can be zero.
If the sum of all the elements of [latex]A[/latex] is at most 2(n-1), then the graph must be acyclic.
If there is at least a 1 in each of A's rows and columns, then the graph must be connected.
questions.solution:
Checking each statement:
- [latex](A^2)_{ii}=\sum_k a_{ik}a_{ki}[/latex] = number of neighbours of i = degree [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE.
- Path 1-2-3 (n = 3): [latex]A^2+I[/latex] has entry (1, 2) = 0, since there is no walk of length exactly 2 from 1 to 2 [latex]\text{---}[/latex] FALSE.
- Sum of entries [latex]\le2(n-1)[/latex] means at most [latex]n-1[/latex] edges. A triangle plus an isolated vertex (n = 4, 3 edges) still has a cycle [latex]\text{---}[/latex] FALSE.
- Two disjoint edges on 4 vertices: every row has a 1, but the graph is disconnected [latex]\text{---}[/latex] FALSE.

Answer: The diagonal entries of [latex]A^2[/latex] are the degrees of the vertices

questions.subject: Engineering Mathematics
questions.text:
Which of the following is/are the eigenvector(s) for the matrix given below?
[latex] \begin{pmatrix} -9 &-6 &-2 &-4 \\ -8& -6 & -3 & -1 \\ 20 & 15 & 8 & 5 \\ 32& 21& 7&12 \end{pmatrix}[/latex]
questions.solution:
Multiply the matrix by each vector and check if the result is a multiple of it:
- [latex](-1,1,0,1)\rightarrow(-1,1,0,1)[/latex] = 1[latex]\cdot[/latex]v True
- [latex](1,0,-1,0)\rightarrow(-7,-5,12,25)[/latex] [latex]\text{---}[/latex] not a multiple False
- [latex](-1,0,2,2)\rightarrow(-3,0,6,6)[/latex] = 3[latex]\cdot[/latex]v True
- [latex](0,1,-3,0)\rightarrow(0,3,-9,0)[/latex] = 3[latex]\cdot[/latex]v True

Answer: Options 1, 3 and 4

questions.subject: Computer Organization
questions.text: Consider a system with 2 KB direct mapped data cache with a block size of 64 bytes. The system has a physical address space of 64 KB and a word length of 16 bits. During the execution of a program, four data words P, Q, R, and S are accessed in that order 10 times (i.e., PQRSPQRS...). Hence, there are 40 accesses to data cache altogether. Assume that the data cache is initially empty and no other data words are accessed by the program. The addresses of the first bytes of P, Q, R, and S are 0xA248, 0xC28A, 0xCA8A, and 0xA262, respectively. For the execution of the above program, which of the following statements is/are TRUE with respect to the data cache?
options: Every access to S is a hit.
Once P is brought to the cache it is never evicted.
At the end of the execution only R and S reside in the cache.
Every access to R evicts Q from the cache.
questions.solution:
Lines = 2 KB / 64 B = 32. Address 16 bits = tag 5 | index 5 | offset 6. Block number = address / 64; line = block mod 32.
- P = 0xA248 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] block 649 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] line 9
- Q = 0xC28A [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] block 778 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] line 10
- R = 0xCA8A [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] block 810 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] line 10
- S = 0xA262 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] block 649 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] line 9 (same block as P)

- S is always accessed after P has loaded that block [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] every S access is a hit True
- Line 9 is used only by P/S [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] P is never evicted True
- Q and R share line 10 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] every R access evicts Q True
- At the end, P's block (with S) and R are in the cache, not "only R and S" False

Answer: Options 1, 2 and 4

questions.subject: Computer Network
questions.text:
Consider routing table of an organization's router shown below:
[latex] \begin{array}{|l|l|l|} Subnet Number & Subnet Mask & Next Hop \\ 12.20.164.0 & 255.255.252.0 & R1 \\ 12.20.170.0 & 255.255.254.0 & R2 \\ 12.20.168.0 & 255.255.254.0 & Interface 0 \\ 12.20.166.0 & 255.255.254.0 & Interface 1 \\ default & ~ & R3 \\ \hline \end{array} [/latex]
Which of the following prefixes in CIDR notation can be collectively used to correctly aggregate all of the subnets in the routing table?
questions.solution:
Third-octet ranges of the subnets:
- 164.0/22 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] 164-167
- 166.0/23 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] 166-167 (inside the first)
- 168.0/23 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] 168-169
- 170.0/23 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] 170-171

Together they cover 164-171. 12.20.164.0/22 covers 164-167 and 12.20.168.0/22 covers 168-171, exactly the needed range.

164.0/21 is really 160-167 (not aligned) and /20 is 160-175, both covering addresses that are not in the table.

Answer: 12.20.164.0/22 and 12.20.168.0/22

questions.text:

questions.subject: Computer Network
questions.text:
Consider a network with three routers P, Q, R shown in the figure below. All the links have cost of unity.

The routers exchange distance vector routing information and have converged on the routing tables, after which the link Q-R fails. Assume that P and Q send out routing updates at random times, each at the same average rate. The probability of a routing loop formation (rounded off to one decimal place) between P and Q, leading to count-to-infinity problem, is ____
questions.solution:
Before failure: Q reaches R at cost 1, P reaches R at cost 2 (via Q). After Q-R fails:
- If Q sends its update first (R unreachable), P learns R is unreachable [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] no loop.
- If P sends first, it still advertises "R at cost 2". Q then sets its route to R via P (cost 3), and P routes through Q [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] routing loop and count-to-infinity.

Both are equally likely, so probability [latex]=0.5[/latex].

Answer: 0.5

questions.subject: Algorithm
questions.text:
Let [latex]G(V, E)[/latex] be a directed graph, where [latex]V = \{1, 2, 3, 4, 5 \}[/latex] is the set of vertices and [latex]E[/latex] is the set of directed edges, as defined by the following adjacency matrix [latex]A[/latex].
[latex]A[i][j]= \left \{ \begin{matrix} 1 &1 \leq j \leq i \leq 5 \\ 0& otherwise \end{matrix} \right.[/latex]
[latex]A[i][j]=1 [/latex]indicates a directed edge from node [latex]i [/latex] to node [latex]j [/latex]. A directed spanning tree of [latex]G [/latex], rooted at [latex] r \in V[/latex] , is defined as a subgraph [latex]T [/latex] of [latex]G [/latex] such that the undirected version of [latex]T [/latex] is a tree, and [latex]T [/latex] contains a directed path from [latex]r [/latex] to every other vertex in [latex]V [/latex]. The number of such directed spanning trees rooted at vertex 5 is ____
questions.solution:
Edge [latex]i\rightarrow j[/latex] exists only when [latex]j\le i[/latex], so edges go from larger to smaller vertices (self-loops are useless in a tree).

In a tree rooted at 5, each other vertex k needs exactly one parent, which must be a vertex larger than k:
- vertex 4: parent 5 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] 1 choice
- vertex 3: 4 or 5 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] 2 choices
- vertex 2: 3 choices
- vertex 1: 4 choices

Parents are always larger, so no cycle can form. Total [latex]=1\times2\times3\times4=24[/latex]

Answer: 24

questions.subject: Computer Network
questions.text: Consider a 100 Mbps link between an earth station (sender) and a satellite (receiver) at an altitude of 2100 km. The signal propagates at a speed of [latex]3  \times 10^8[/latex] m/s. The time taken (in milliseconds, rounded off to two decimal places) for the receiver to completely receive a packet of 1000 bytes transmitted by the sender is
questions.solution:
Total time = transmission time + propagation time.
- Transmission time [latex]=\frac{1000\times8}{100\times10^6}=0.08[/latex] ms
- Propagation time [latex]=\frac{2100\times10^3}{3\times10^8}=7[/latex] ms

Total [latex]=0.08+7=7.08[/latex] ms

Answer: 7.08

questions.subject: Computer Network
questions.text: Consider the data transfer using TCP over a 1 Gbps link. Assuming that the maximum segment lifetime (MSL) is set to 60 seconds, the minimum number of bits required for the sequence number field of the TCP header, to prevent the sequence number space from wrapping around during the MSL is
questions.solution:
TCP numbers bytes. Bytes sent in one MSL:
[latex]\frac{10^9\times60}{8}=7.5\times10^9[/latex] bytes

We need [latex]2^k\ge7.5\times10^9[/latex]. [latex]2^{32}\approx4.29\times10^9[/latex] (too small), [latex]2^{33}\approx8.59\times10^9[/latex] (enough).

Answer: 33

questions.subject: Computer Organization
questions.text: A processor [latex]X_1[/latex] operating at 2 GHz has a standard 5-stage RISC instruction pipeline having a base CPI (cycles per instruction) of one without any pipeline hazards. For a given program P that has 30% branch instructions, control hazards incur 2 cycles stall for every branch. A new version of the processor [latex]X_2[/latex] operating at same clock frequency has an additional branch predictor unit (BPU) that completely eliminates stalls for correctly predicted branches. There is neither any savings nor any additional stalls for wrong predictions. There are no structural hazards and data hazards for [latex]X_1[/latex] and [latex]X_2[/latex]. If the BPU has a prediction accuracy of 80%, the speed up (rounded   off to   two decimal places)   obtained   by [latex]X_2[/latex]    over   [latex]X_1[/latex]   in executing P is
questions.solution:
Compare the CPI of both processors:
- [latex]X_1[/latex]: CPI [latex]=1+0.3\times2=1.6[/latex]
- [latex]X_2[/latex]: only the 20% wrongly predicted branches stall: CPI [latex]=1+0.3\times0.2\times2=1.12[/latex]

Same clock, so speedup [latex]=\frac{1.6}{1.12}\approx1.43[/latex]

Answer: 1.43

questions.subject: Data Structure
questions.text: Consider the queues Q1 containing four elements and Q2 containing none (shown as the Initial State in the figure). The only operations allowed on these two queues are [latex]Enqueue(Q,element)[/latex] and [latex]Dequeue(Q)[/latex]. The minimum number of [latex]Enqueue [/latex] operations on Q1 required to place the elements of Q1 in Q2 in reverse order (shown as the Final State in the figure) without using any additional storage is
questions.solution:
Use only Q2 for the reversal: after enqueueing each new element into Q2, rotate the older elements behind it (dequeue from Q2 and enqueue into Q2).
- Move 1 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] Q2: [1]
- Move 2 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] Q2: [1, 2], rotate once [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] [2, 1]
- Move 3 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] Q2, rotate twice [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] [3, 2, 1]
- Move 4 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] Q2, rotate 3 times [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] [4, 3, 2, 1]

Q1 is only dequeued, never enqueued.

Answer: 0

questions.subject: Operating System
questions.text:
Consider two files systems A and B , that use contiguous allocation and linked allocation, respectively. A file of size 100 blocks is already stored in A and also in
B. Now, consider inserting a new block in the middle of the file (between [latex]50^{th}  \text{ and }51^{st}[/latex] block), whose data is already available in the memory. Assume that there are enough free blocks at the end of the file and that the file control blocks are already in memory. Let the number of disk accesses required to insert a block in the middle of the file in   A   and     B   are [latex]n_A[/latex] and [latex]n_B[/latex],   respectively, then the value of  [latex]n_A+n_B[/latex]  is
questions.solution:
Contiguous (A): blocks 51-100 must each move one place: read + write for 50 blocks = 100 accesses, plus writing the new block = 1. [latex]n_A=101[/latex].

Linked (B): follow pointers to reach block 50 = 50 reads; write the new block (pointing to block 51) = 1; rewrite block 50's pointer = 1. [latex]n_B=52[/latex].

[latex]n_A+n_B=101+52=153[/latex]

Answer: 153

questions.subject: Operating System
questions.text:
Consider a demand paging system with four page frames (initially empty) and LRU page replacement policy. For the following page reference string

7, 2, 7, 3, 2, 5, 3, 4, 6, 7, 7,1, 5, 6,1

the page fault rate, defined as the ratio of number of page faults to the number of memory accesses (rounded off to one decimal place) is
questions.solution:
LRU with 4 frames (F = fault):
7 F, 2 F, 7 hit, 3 F, 2 hit, 5 F [7, 2, 3, 5], 3 hit,
4 F (evict 7), 6 F (evict 2), 7 F (evict 5), 7 hit, 1 F (evict 3), 5 F (evict 4), 6 hit, 1 hit.

Faults = 9 out of 15 references. Rate [latex]=\frac{9}{15}=0.6[/latex]

Answer: 0.6

questions.subject: Compiler Design
questions.text:
Consider the following grammar along with translation rules.
[latex] \begin{aligned} &S \rightarrow S_1 \# T & & \{S._{val}=S_{1.val}*T._{val} \} \\ &S \rightarrow T & & \{S._{val}=T._{val} \} \\ &T \rightarrow T_1 \% R & & \{T._{val}=T_{1.val} \div R._{val} \} \\ &T \rightarrow R & & \{T._{val}=R._{val} \} \\ &R \rightarrow id & & \{R._{val}=id._{val} \} \\ \end{aligned}[/latex]
Here [latex] \#[/latex] and [latex] \%[/latex] are operators and [latex]id[/latex] is a token that represents an integer and [latex]id_{.val}[/latex] represents the corresponding integer value. The set of non-terminals is [latex] \{S,T,R,P \}[/latex] and a subscripted non-terminal indicates an instance of the non-terminal.
Using this translation scheme, the computed value of [latex]S_{.val}[/latex] for root of the parse tree for the expression [latex]20 \# 10 \% 5 \# 8 \% 2 \% 2[/latex] is
questions.solution:
From the grammar, # (multiply) is at the S level, so it has lower precedence; % (divide) is at the T level, so it binds tighter. Both are left recursive, i.e. left associative.

[latex]20\,\#\,(10\%5)\,\#\,((8\%2)\%2)=20\times2\times2=80[/latex]

Answer: 80

questions.subject: General Aptitude
questions.text: The _____ is too high for it to be considered ______
questions.solution:
Fare = price of a ticket/journey; fair = reasonable / just.

"The fare is too high for it to be considered fair."

Answer: fare / fair

questions.subject: General Aptitude
questions.text:
A function [latex]y(x)[/latex] is defined in the interval [0, 1] on the [latex]x-[/latex]axis as
[latex]y(x)= \left \{ \begin{matrix} 2 &if & 0 \leq x \leq \frac{1}{3} \\ 3& if& \frac{1}{3} \leq x \leq \frac{3}{4} \\ 1& if& \frac{3}{4} \leq x \leq 1 \end{matrix} \right.[/latex]
Which one of the following is the area under the curve for the interval [0, 1] on the [latex]x-[/latex]axis?
questions.solution:
Area = sum of (height [latex]\times[/latex] width) of each piece:
[latex]2\times\frac13+3\times\left(\frac34-\frac13\right)+1\times\frac14=\frac{8}{12}+\frac{15}{12}+\frac{3}{12}=\frac{26}{12}=\frac{13}{6}[/latex]

Answer: [latex]\frac{13}{6}[/latex]

questions.subject: General Aptitude
questions.text:
Let [latex]r[/latex] be a root of the equation [latex]x^2+2x+6=0[/latex]
Then the value of the expression [latex](r+2)(r+3)(r+4)(r+5)[/latex] is
questions.solution:
Pair the factors: [latex](r+2)(r+5)=r^2+7r+10[/latex] and [latex](r+3)(r+4)=r^2+7r+12[/latex].

From [latex]r^2=-2r-6[/latex]: these become [latex]5r+4[/latex] and [latex]5r+6[/latex].

[latex](5r+4)(5r+6)=25r^2+50r+24=25(r^2+2r)+24=25(-6)+24=-126[/latex]

Answer: -126

questions.subject: General Aptitude
questions.text:
Given below are four statements.

Statement 1: All students are inquisitive.
Statement 2: Some students are inquisitive.
Statement 3: No student is inquisitive.
Statement 4: Some students are not inquisitive.

From the given four statements, find the two statements that CANNOT BE TRUE simultaneously, assuming that there is at least one student in the class.
questions.solution:
"All students are inquisitive" and "No student is inquisitive" directly contradict each other (there is at least one student), so they can never both be true.

Every other pair can hold together (e.g. statements 2 and 4 hold when some are and some are not inquisitive).

Answer: Statement 1 and Statement 3

questions.subject: General Aptitude
questions.text:
A palindrome is a word that reads the same forwards and backwards. In a game of words, a player has the following two plates painted with letters.

From the additional plates given in the options, which one of the combinations of additional plates would allow the player to construct a five-letter palindrome. The player should use all the five plates exactly once. The plates can be rotated in their plane.
questions.solution:
A 5-letter palindrome has the form X Y Z Y X, so letters must pair up around a middle letter. We already have A and D.

Option B gives R, an upside-down A and a mirrored R. Rotating the plates gives R, A, R, which makes R A D A R [latex]\text{---}[/latex] a palindrome using all 5 plates.

The other options cannot form matching pairs around a middle letter.

Answer: B

questions.subject: General Aptitude
questions.text:
Some people believe that "what gets measured, improves". Some others believe that "what gets measured, gets gamed". One possible reason for the difference in the beliefs is the work culture in organizations. In organizations with good work culture, metrics help improve outcomes. However, the same metrics are counterproductive in organizations with poor work culture.
Which one of the following is the CORRECT logical inference based on the information in the above passage?
options: Metrics are useful in organizations with poor work culture
Metrics are useful in organizations with good work culture
Metrics are always counterproductive in organizations with good work culture
Metrics are never useful in organizations with good work culture
questions.solution:
The passage says: in organizations with good work culture, metrics help improve outcomes; with poor culture they are counterproductive.

So the direct inference is that metrics are useful in organizations with good work culture. Options 1, 3 and 4 contradict the passage.

Answer: Metrics are useful in organizations with good work culture

questions.subject: General Aptitude
questions.text:
In a recently conducted national entrance test, boys constituted 65% of those who appeared for the test. Girls constituted the remaining candidates and they accounted for 60% of the qualified candidates.
Which one of the following is the correct logical inference based on the information provided in the above passage?
options: Equal number of boys and girls qualified
Equal number of boys and girls appeared for the test
The number of boys who appeared for the test is less than the number of girls who appeared
The number of boys who qualified the test is less than the number of girls who qualified
questions.solution:
Girls are 60% of the qualified candidates, so boys are only 40% of them. Hence fewer boys than girls qualified.

(Boys were 65% of those who appeared, so the options about who appeared are wrong, and the qualified numbers are not equal.)

Answer: The number of boys who qualified the test is less than the number of girls who qualified

questions.subject: General Aptitude
questions.text:
A box contains five balls of same size and shape. Three of them are green coloured balls and two of them are orange coloured balls. Balls are drawn from the box one at a time. If a green ball is drawn, it is not replaced. If an orange ball is drawn, it is replaced with another orange ball.
First ball is drawn. What is the probability of getting an orange ball in the next draw?
questions.solution:
Start: 3 green, 2 orange.
- First green ([latex]\frac35[/latex]): it is not replaced [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] 2G, 2O [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] P(orange) = [latex]\frac24[/latex]
- First orange ([latex]\frac25[/latex]): replaced [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] 3G, 2O [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] P(orange) = [latex]\frac25[/latex]

[latex]P=\frac35\cdot\frac12+\frac25\cdot\frac25=\frac{15}{50}+\frac{8}{50}=\frac{23}{50}[/latex]

Answer: [latex]\frac{23}{50}[/latex]

questions.subject: General Aptitude
questions.text:
The corners and mid-points of the sides of a triangle are named using the distinct letters P, Q, R, S, T and U, but not necessarily in the same order. Consider the following statements:

The line joining P and R is parallel to the line joining Q and S.
P is placed on the side opposite to the corner T.
S and U cannot be placed on the same side.

Which one of the following statements is correct based on the above information?
options: P cannot be placed at a corner
S cannot be placed at a corner
U cannot be placed at a mid-point
R cannot be placed at a corner
questions.solution:
In a triangle, two such lines can be parallel only if one joins two midpoints and the other lies along the opposite side.

- If Q and S are the two midpoints, S is a midpoint.
- Otherwise P and R are the midpoints, and Q, S lie on the parallel side (its two corners and its midpoint). P sits on the side opposite T, so T is also a point of that side, and U is the remaining corner. S cannot share a side with U, and both corners of that side share a side with U. So S must be the midpoint.

In every case S is a midpoint.

Answer: S cannot be placed at a corner

questions.subject: General Aptitude
questions.text: A plot of land must be divided between four families. They want their individual plots to be similar in shape, not necessarily equal in area. The land has equally spaced poles, marked as dots in the below figure. Two ropes, R1 and R2, are already present and cannot be moved. What is the least number of additional straight ropes needed to create the desired plots? A single rope can pass through three poles that are aligned in a straight line.
questions.solution:
Take the poles as a 7 [latex]\times[/latex] 7 grid (0-6). R1 runs from the left edge (0, 2) to (2, 2), R2 from the top edge (4, 6) to (4, 4). The land is symmetric about both diagonals, and R1, R2 are mirror images.

Add 3 ropes:
1. (2, 0) to (2, 2) [latex]\text{---}[/latex] mirror of R1
2. (6, 4) to (4, 4) [latex]\text{---}[/latex] mirror of R2
3. (2, 2) to (4, 4) [latex]\text{---}[/latex] diagonal through the centre pole (3, 3)

This gives two small plots (a 2[latex]\times[/latex]2 square with one corner cut) and two large plots (a 4[latex]\times[/latex]4 square with one corner cut). The large ones are exactly the small ones scaled by 2, so all four are similar. Two ropes cannot do this.

Answer: 3

questions.subject: Compiler Design
questions.text:
Consider the following statements regarding the front-end and back-end of a compiler.

S1: The front-end includes phases that are independent of the target hardware.
S2: The back-end includes phases that are specific to the target hardware.
S3: The back-end includes phases that are specific to the programming language used in the source code.

Identify the CORRECT option.
options: Only S1 and S2 are TRUE.
S1, S2, and S3 are all TRUE.
Only S1 and S3 are TRUE.
questions.solution:
Checking each statement:
- Front end (lexical, syntax, semantic analysis, intermediate code) depends on the source language, not on the target machine [latex]\text{---}[/latex] S1 TRUE.
- Back end (code optimization for the machine, code generation) is specific to the target hardware [latex]\text{---}[/latex] S2 TRUE.
- The back end works on intermediate code, so it is independent of the source language [latex]\text{---}[/latex] S3 FALSE.

Answer: Only S1 and S2 are TRUE

questions.subject: Data Structure
questions.text:
Which one of the following sequences when stored in an array at locations
A[1], . . . , A[10] forms a max-heap?
questions.solution:
Max-heap: every parent [latex]A[i]\ge[/latex] its children [latex]A[2i][/latex], [latex]A[2i+1][/latex].

- Option 1: A[3] = 10 has child A[6] = 14 False
- Option 2: 23 [latex]\ge[/latex] 17, 14; 17 [latex]\ge[/latex] 7, 13; 14 [latex]\ge[/latex] 10, 1; 7 [latex]\ge[/latex] 5, 6; 13 [latex]\ge[/latex] 12 True
- Option 3: A[5] = 13 has child A[10] = 15 False
- Option 4: A[4] = 1 has children 12, 7 False

Answer: 23, 17, 14, 7, 13, 10, 1, 5, 6, 12

questions.subject: Data Structure
questions.text:
Let SLLdel be a function that deletes a node in a singly-linked list given a pointer to the node and a pointer to the head of the list. Similarly, let DLLdel be another function that deletes a node in a doubly-linked list given a pointer to the node and a pointer to the head of the list.
Let n denote the number of nodes in each of the linked lists. Which one of the following choices is TRUE about the worst-case time complexity of SLLdel and DLLdel?
options: SLLdel is O(1) and DLLdel is O(n)
Both SLLdel and DLLdel are O(log(n))
Both SLLdel and DLLdel are O(1)
SLLdel is O(n) and DLLdel is O(1)
questions.solution:
To delete a node we must update its predecessor's next pointer.

- Singly linked list: the predecessor is found only by walking from the head [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] [latex]O(n)[/latex].
- Doubly linked list: the node's prev pointer gives the predecessor directly [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] [latex]O(1)[/latex].

Answer: SLLdel is O(n) and DLLdel is O(1)

questions.subject: Theory of Computation
questions.text:
Consider the Deterministic Finite-state Automaton (DFA) [latex]A[/latex] shown below. The DFA runs on the alphabet {0, 1}, and has the set of states {s, p, q, r}, with s being the start state and p being the only final state.

Which one of the following regular expressions correctly describes the language accepted by [latex]A[/latex]?
questions.solution:
From s: 0 goes to dead state r, so a string must start with 1 (reaching final state p).
At p: 0 loops on p; 1 goes to q, and from q only another 1 returns to p (0 goes to r).

So after the first 1, we repeat "0" or "11": [latex]1(0+11)^*[/latex].

Answer: [latex]1(0+11)^*[/latex]

questions.subject: Discrete Mathematics
questions.text:
The Lucas sequence [latex] L_n [/latex] is defined by the recurrence relation:
[latex] L_n=L_{n-1}+L_{n-2}, \; for \; n\geq 3, [/latex]
with [latex] L_1=1 \; and \; L_2=3 [/latex]
Which one of the options given is TRUE?
questions.solution:
Let [latex]\varphi=\frac{1+\sqrt5}{2}[/latex] and [latex]\psi=\frac{1-\sqrt5}{2}[/latex]. They satisfy [latex]x^2=x+1[/latex], [latex]\varphi+\psi=1[/latex], [latex]\varphi\psi=-1[/latex].

Check [latex]L_n=\varphi^n+\psi^n[/latex]:
- [latex]L_1=\varphi+\psi=1[/latex] True
- [latex]L_2=(\varphi+\psi)^2-2\varphi\psi=1+2=3[/latex] True
- It satisfies [latex]L_n=L_{n-1}+L_{n-2}[/latex] because both [latex]\varphi,\psi[/latex] satisfy [latex]x^2=x+1[/latex].

Answer: [latex]L_n=\left(\frac{1+\sqrt5}{2}\right)^n+\left(\frac{1-\sqrt5}{2}\right)^n[/latex]

questions.subject: Database Management System
questions.text:
Which one of the options given below refers to the degree (or arity) of a relation in
relational database systems?
options: Number of attributes of its relation schema.
Number of tuples stored in the relation.
Number of entries in the relation.
Number of distinct domains of its relation schema.
questions.solution:
Degree (arity) = number of attributes (columns) in the relation schema.
The number of tuples (rows) is called the cardinality.

Answer: Number of attributes of its relation schema

questions.subject: Computer Network
questions.text:
Suppose two hosts are connected by a point-to-point link and they are configured
to use Stop-and-Wait protocol for reliable data transfer. Identify in which one of
the following scenarios, the utilization of the link is the lowest.
options: Longer link length and lower transmission rate
Longer link length and higher transmission rate
Shorter link length and lower transmission rate
Shorter link length and higher transmission rate
questions.solution:
Stop-and-wait utilization [latex]=\frac{T_t}{T_t+2T_p}=\frac{1}{1+2a}[/latex], where [latex]a=\frac{T_p}{T_t}[/latex].

Utilization is lowest when [latex]a[/latex] is largest:
- longer link [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] larger [latex]T_p[/latex]
- higher transmission rate [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] smaller [latex]T_t[/latex]

Answer: Longer link length and higher transmission rate

questions.subject: Engineering Mathematics
questions.text:
Let [latex] A=\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 & 3 &4 \\ 4& 1& 2 &3 \\ 3& 4 & 1 &2 \\ 2 &3 &4 &1 \end{bmatrix}[/latex] and [latex] B=\begin{bmatrix} 3& 4 & 1 &2 \\ 4& 1& 2 &3 \\ 1 & 2 & 3 &4 \\ 2 &3 &4 &1 \end{bmatrix}[/latex]
Let det(A) and det(B) denote the determinants of the matrices A and B, respectively.
Which one of the options given below is TRUE?
questions.solution:
Rows of B are rows of A in the order [latex]R_3,R_2,R_1,R_4[/latex], i.e. B is A with rows 1 and 3 swapped.

One row swap changes the sign of the determinant: [latex]\det(B)=-\det(A)[/latex].

Answer: det(B) = [latex]-[/latex]det(A)

questions.subject: Theory of Computation
questions.text:
Consider the following definition of a lexical token [latex]id[/latex] for an identifier in a programming language, using extended regular expressions:

[latex] letter \rightarrow [A-Za-z][/latex]
[latex] digit \rightarrow [0-9][/latex]
[latex] id \rightarrow letter (letter\;| \;digit)^*[/latex]


Which one of the following Non-deterministic Finite-state Automata with - transitions accepts the set of valid identifiers? (A double-circle denotes a final state)
questions.solution:
An identifier is one letter followed by any mix of letters and digits.

- (A): the [latex]\epsilon[/latex] edge lets the string skip the first letter, e.g. "1" or the empty string is accepted [latex]\text{---}[/latex] wrong.
- (B): after choosing a branch you stay with only letters or only digits; "a1b" is rejected [latex]\text{---}[/latex] wrong.
- (C): letter, then from the final state any number of letter-or-digit steps through the loop [latex]\text{---}[/latex] correct.
- (D): forces "letter digit" pairs; "ab" is rejected [latex]\text{---}[/latex] wrong.

Answer: C

questions.subject: Data Structure
questions.text:
An algorithm has to store several keys generated by an adversary in a hash table. The adversary is malicious who tries to maximize the number of collisions. Let [latex] k[/latex] be the number of keys, [latex] m[/latex] be the number of slots in the hash table, and [latex] k \gt m[/latex].
Which one of the following is the best hashing strategy to counteract the adversary?
options: Division method, i.e., use the hash function [latex]h(k) = k\;  mod \; m[/latex]

Multiplication method, i.e., use the hash function [latex] h(k) =  \left \lfloor m(kA -\left \lfloor kA \right \rfloor ) \right \rfloor[/latex], where
[latex]A[/latex] is a carefully chosen constant.
If [latex]k[/latex] is a prime number, use Division method. Otherwise, use Multiplication method
questions.solution:
Any fixed hash function (division or multiplication) is known to the adversary, who can pick keys that all collide.

Universal hashing picks the hash function at random from a family at run time, so the adversary cannot predict it, and the expected number of collisions stays small.

Answer: Universal hashing method

questions.subject: Digital Logic
questions.text:
The output of a 2-input multiplexer is connected back to one of its inputs as shown in the figure.

Match the functional equivalence of this circuit to one of the following options.
questions.solution:
The output Q is fed back to input 0.
- S = 1: Q follows input 1 (the data input D).
- S = 0: Q = Q, so it holds its old value.

It is transparent while S = 1 and holds while S = 0, which is a level-triggered D latch (S acts as enable). There is no clock edge, so it is not a flip-flop.

Answer: D Latch

questions.subject: Operating System
questions.text:
Which one or more of the following need to be saved on a context switch from one
thread (T1) of a process to another thread (T2) of the same process?
questions.solution:
Threads of the same process share the address space, so the page table base register does not change and need not be saved.

Each thread has its own execution context: stack pointer, program counter and general purpose registers [latex]\text{---}[/latex] these must be saved.

Answer: Stack pointer, Program counter, General purpose registers

questions.subject: Operating System
questions.text:
Which one or more of the following options guarantee that a computer system will
transition from user mode to kernel mode?
questions.solution:
Check which events always enter the kernel:
- Function call: runs entirely in user mode [latex]\text{---}[/latex] no switch.
- malloc: a library function; it usually takes memory from the existing heap and makes a system call only sometimes [latex]\text{---}[/latex] not guaranteed.
- Page fault: an exception handled by the OS [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] always kernel mode.
- System call: a trap into the kernel [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] always kernel mode.

Answer: Page Fault, System Call

questions.subject: Theory of Computation
questions.text: Which of the following statements is/are CORRECT?
options: The intersection of two regular languages is regular.
The intersection of two context-free languages is context-free.
The intersection of two recursive languages is recursive.
The intersection of two recursively enumerable languages is recursively enumerable.
questions.solution:
Checking each statement:
- Regular languages are closed under intersection [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE.
- CFLs are not closed under intersection: [latex]a^nb^nc^m\cap a^mb^nc^n=a^nb^nc^n[/latex] [latex]\text{---}[/latex] FALSE.
- Recursive: run both deciders, accept if both accept [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE.
- RE: run both recognizers, accept when both accept [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE.

Answer: Options 1, 3 and 4

questions.subject: Computer Network
questions.text:
Which of the following statements is/are INCORRECT about
the OSPF (Open Shortest Path First) routing protocol used in the Internet?
options: OSPF implements Bellman-Ford algorithm to find shortest paths.
OSPF uses Dijkstra's shortest path algorithm to implement least-cost path routing
OSPF is used as an inter-domain routing protocol
questions.solution:
OSPF is a link-state protocol.
- "Implements Bellman-Ford": it uses Dijkstra (Bellman-Ford is for distance vector, like RIP) [latex]\text{---}[/latex] INCORRECT.
- "Uses Dijkstra" [latex]\text{---}[/latex] correct.
- "Inter-domain protocol": OSPF is intra-domain (inside one AS); BGP is inter-domain [latex]\text{---}[/latex] INCORRECT.
- "Hierarchical routing" with areas and a backbone [latex]\text{---}[/latex] correct.

Answer: Options 1 and 3

questions.subject: Discrete Mathematics
questions.text:
Geetha has a conjecture about integers, which is of the form
[latex]\forall x\left [P(x)\Rightarrow \exists yQ(x,y) \right ] [/latex]
where [latex]P[/latex] is a statement about integers, and [latex]Q[/latex] is a statement about pairs of integers. Which of the following (one or more) option(s) would imply Geetha's conjecture?
questions.solution:
Conjecture: for every x with P(x), some y makes Q(x, y) true.

- Option 1 talks about only one x [latex]\text{---}[/latex] does not imply it.
- Option 2: Q holds for all x and y, so for any x any y works [latex]\text{---}[/latex] implies it.
- Option 3: one fixed y works for every x with P(x), so such a y exists for each x [latex]\text{---}[/latex] implies it.
- Option 4 again talks about only one x [latex]\text{---}[/latex] does not imply it.

Answer: Options 2 and 3

questions.subject: Operating System
questions.text:
Which one or more of the following CPU scheduling algorithms can potentially
cause starvation?
questions.solution:
Check whether a process can wait forever:
- FIFO: every process eventually reaches the front [latex]\text{---}[/latex] no starvation.
- Round Robin: each process gets a time slice every round [latex]\text{---}[/latex] no starvation.
- Priority scheduling: a low-priority process may wait forever if high-priority processes keep arriving.
- SJF: a long job may wait forever if short jobs keep arriving.

Answer: Priority Scheduling, Shortest Job First

questions.subject: Engineering Mathematics
questions.text:
Let [latex]f(x)=x^3+15x^2-33x-36 [/latex] be a real-valued function.
Which of the following statements is/are TRUE?
options: [latex]f(x)[/latex] does not have a local maximum.
[latex]f(x)[/latex] does not have a local minimum.
questions.solution:
[latex]f'(x)=3x^2+30x-33=3(x^2+10x-11)=3(x+11)(x-1)[/latex] [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] critical points [latex]x=-11[/latex] and [latex]x=1[/latex].

[latex]f''(x)=6x+30[/latex]:
- [latex]f''(-11)=-36 \lt 0[/latex] [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] local maximum
- [latex]f''(1)=36 \gt 0[/latex] [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] local minimum

Answer: f(x) has a local maximum and has a local minimum

questions.subject: Algorithm
questions.text:
Let [latex]f[/latex] and [latex]g[/latex] be functions of natural numbers given by [latex]f(n)=n[/latex] and [latex]g(n)=n^2[/latex].
Which of the following statements is/are TRUE?
questions.solution:
[latex]\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{f(n)}{g(n)}=\lim\frac{n}{n^2}=0[/latex], so f grows strictly slower than g.

- [latex]f\in O(g)[/latex] [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE
- [latex]f\in o(g)[/latex] (strictly smaller) [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE
- [latex]f\in\Omega(g)[/latex] and [latex]f\in\Theta(g)[/latex] [latex]\text{---}[/latex] FALSE

Answer: [latex]f\in O(g)[/latex] and [latex]f\in o(g)[/latex]

questions.subject: Engineering Mathematics
questions.text:
Let A be the adjacency matrix of the graph with vertices {1, 2, 3, 4, 5}.

Let [latex]\lambda _1,\lambda _2,\lambda _3,\lambda _4,\; and \; \lambda _5[/latex] be the five eigenvalues of A. Note that these eigenvalues need not be distinct.
The value of [latex]\lambda _1+\lambda _2+\lambda _3+ \lambda _4+ \lambda _5 =[/latex] _____
questions.solution:
Sum of eigenvalues = trace of A = sum of the diagonal entries.

A diagonal entry [latex]a_{ii}[/latex] is 1 only if vertex i has a self-loop. In the graph, vertices 3 and 4 have self-loops, so trace [latex]=1+1=2[/latex].

Answer: 2

questions.subject: Engineering Mathematics
questions.text: The value of the definite integral [latex] \int_{-3}^{3}  \int_{-2}^{2}  \int_{-1}^{1} (4x^2y-z^3)dzdydx[/latex] is _____. (Rounded off to the nearest integer)
questions.solution:
Split the integrand:
- [latex]4x^2y[/latex]: odd in y, integrated over the symmetric range [latex][-2,2][/latex] [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] 0
- [latex]z^3[/latex]: odd in z, integrated over [latex][-1,1][/latex] [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] 0

Total = 0

Answer: 0

questions.subject: Digital Logic
questions.text:
A particular number is written as 132 in radix-4 representation. The same number
in radix-5 representation is _____.
questions.solution:
[latex](132)_4=1\times16+3\times4+2=30[/latex]

Convert 30 to base 5: [latex]30=1\times25+1\times5+0[/latex] [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] [latex](110)_5[/latex]

Answer: 110

questions.subject: Computer Organization
questions.text:
Consider a 3-stage pipelined processor having a delay of 10 ns (nanoseconds), 20 ns, and 14 ns, for the first, second, and the third stages, respectively. Assume that there is no other delay and the processor does not suffer from any pipeline hazards. Also assume that one instruction is fetched every cycle.
The total execution time for executing 100 instructions on this processor is _______ ns
questions.solution:
Cycle time = slowest stage = 20 ns.
Total cycles for n instructions on k stages = [latex]k+n-1=3+100-1=102[/latex].

Time [latex]=102\times20=2040[/latex] ns

Answer: 2040

questions.subject: Computer Organization
questions.text:
A keyboard connected to a computer is used at a rate of 1 keystroke per second. The computer system polls the keyboard every 10 ms (milli seconds) to check for a keystroke and consumes 100 [latex] \mu s[/latex] (micro seconds) for each poll. If it is determined after polling that a key has been pressed, the system consumes an additional 200 [latex] \mu s[/latex] to process the keystroke. Let [latex] T_1[/latex] denote the fraction of a second spent in polling and processing a keystroke.
In an alternative implementation, the system uses interrupts instead of polling. An interrupt is raised for every keystroke. It takes a total of 1 ms for servicing an interrupt and processing a keystroke. Let [latex] T_2[/latex] denote the fraction of a second spent in servicing the interrupt and processing a keystroke. The ratio [latex] \frac{T_1}{T_2}[/latex] is ______ . (Rounded off to one decimal place)
questions.solution:
Polling: 100 polls per second (every 10 ms) [latex]\times[/latex] 100 [latex]\mu[/latex]s = 10 ms, plus 200 [latex]\mu[/latex]s for the one keystroke [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] [latex]T_1=10.2[/latex] ms per second.

Interrupts: one keystroke per second [latex]\times[/latex] 1 ms [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] [latex]T_2=1[/latex] ms per second.

[latex]\frac{T_1}{T_2}=\frac{10.2}{1}=10.2[/latex]

Answer: 10.2

questions.subject: C Programming
questions.solution:
static x in funcp keeps its value between calls (starts at 1).
- x = funcp() [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] static x becomes 2 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] x = 2
- y = funcp() + x [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] static x becomes 3 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] y = 3 + 2 = 5

x + y = 7

Answer: 7

questions.subject: C Programming
questions.solution:
Trace the calls:
- main calls f1(), f2(2), f3() [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] 3 children.
- f2(2) calls f3(), then since X [latex]\ne[/latex] 1, calls f2(1).
- f2(1) calls f3(), then since X == 1, calls f1().

Tree: main [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] {f1, f2, f3}; f2 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] {f3, f2}; inner f2 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] {f3, f1}. This matches (A).

Answer: A

questions.subject: Compiler Design
questions.text:
Consider the control flow graph shown.

Which one of the following choices correctly lists the set of live variables at the exit point of each basic block?
questions.solution:
Uses / definitions: B1 defines i, j, a; B2 uses and defines i, j; B3 defines a; B4 uses a and defines i. B4 goes to B2 or exit.

- [latex]IN(B2)=\{i,j\}\cup(OUT(B2)-\{i,j\})[/latex]
- [latex]IN(B4)=\{a\}\cup(OUT(B4)-\{i\})[/latex], [latex]IN(B3)=OUT(B3)-\{a\}[/latex]

Iterating to a fixed point:
- OUT(B4) = IN(B2) = {a, i, j}
- IN(B4) = {a, j} = OUT(B3); IN(B3) = {j}
- OUT(B2) = IN(B3) [latex]\cup[/latex] IN(B4) = {a, j}
- OUT(B1) = IN(B2) = {a, i, j}

Answer: B1: {a, i, j}, B2: {a, j}, B3: {a, j}, B4: {a, i, j}

questions.subject: Operating System
questions.solution:
I-1 (binary semaphore = 1): mutual exclusion, so every update is applied: [latex]V_1=10+5-3=12[/latex].

I-2 (counting semaphore = 2): two threads can be inside together and updates can be lost. To get the minimum:
- a decr thread reads X = 10 and is preempted;
- all 5 incr threads run one after another (using the second slot): X = 15;
- the first decr writes 10 [latex]-[/latex] 1 = 9, wiping out all 5 increments;
- the other 2 decr run normally: X = 7.

So [latex]V_2=7[/latex].

Answer: 12, 7

questions.subject: Theory of Computation
questions.text:
Consider the context-free grammar [latex]G[/latex] below
[latex] S\rightarrow aSb \;| \;X[/latex]
[latex] X\rightarrow aX \;| \;Xb \;|\; a\;|\; b[/latex]
where [latex]S[/latex] and [latex]X[/latex] are non-terminals, and [latex]a[/latex] and [latex]b[/latex] are terminal symbols. The starting non-terminal is [latex]S[/latex].
Which one of the following statements is CORRECT?
options: The language generated by [latex] G \text{ is }(a + b)^*[/latex]
The language generated by [latex] G \text{ is } a^*(a + b)b^*[/latex]
The language generated by [latex] G \text{ is }a^*b^*(a + b)[/latex]
The language generated by [latex] G[/latex] is not a regular language
questions.solution:
X: [latex]X\rightarrow aX[/latex] adds a's on the left, [latex]X\rightarrow Xb[/latex] adds b's on the right, ending with a or b. So [latex]L(X)=a^*(a+b)b^*[/latex].

[latex]S\rightarrow aSb[/latex] only adds more a's on the left and more b's on the right of X, so the result stays in [latex]a^*(a+b)b^*[/latex] and covers all of it (use S [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] X directly).

This is regular, and it is not [latex](a+b)^*[/latex] (e.g. "ba" is missing).

Answer: The language generated by G is [latex]a^*(a+b)b^*[/latex]

questions.subject: Theory of Computation
questions.text:
