Consider the pushdown automaton (PDA) [latex]P[/latex] below, which runs on the input alphabet [latex]\{a,b\}[/latex], has stack alphabet [latex] \{ \perp ,A\}[/latex], and has three states [latex] \{s,p,q\}[/latex], with [latex]s[/latex] being the start state. A transition from state [latex]u[/latex] to state [latex]v[/latex] , labelled [latex]c/X/\gamma [/latex] , where [latex]c[/latex] is an input symbol or , [latex]X[/latex] is a stack symbol, and [latex]\gamma [/latex] is a string of stack symbols, represents the fact that in state [latex]u[/latex], the PDA can read [latex]c[/latex] from the input, with [latex]X[/latex] on the top of its stack, pop [latex]X[/latex] from the stack, push in the string [latex]\gamma [/latex] on the stack, and go to state [latex]v[/latex]. In the initial configuration, the stack has only the symbol [latex]\perp [/latex] in it. The PDA accepts by empty stack.

Which one of the following options correctly describes the language accepted by [latex]P[/latex]?
questions.solution:
Read the PDA transitions:
- In s, every a pushes an A (so m a's give m A's).
- The first b moves to p and pops an A; each further b pops another A.
- To empty the stack we must go to q, and both moves into q need an A on top. In q, the remaining A's and [latex]\perp[/latex] are popped.

So at least one A must be left after reading the b's: [latex]n \lt m[/latex], and [latex]m\ge1[/latex] (with no a's there is no A to move to q).

Answer: [latex]\{a^mb^n\mid 1\le m,\ n \lt m\}[/latex]

questions.subject: Computer Organization
questions.text:
Consider the given C-code and its corresponding assembly code, with a few operands U1-U4 being unknown. Some useful information as well as the semantics of each unique assembly instruction is annotated as inline comments in the code. The memory is byte-addressable.

Which one of the following options is a CORRECT replacement for operands in the position (U1, U2, U3, U4) in the above assembly code?
questions.solution:
Match the C code with the assembly code:
- [latex]b[i]*8[/latex] = shift left by 3 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] U1 = 3.
- int is 4 bytes and memory is byte addressable, so to move to the next element of a and b, add 4 to the pointers: U2 = 4, U3 = 4.
- After incrementing i (r1), jump back to the loop check at L01 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] U4 = L01.

Answer: (3, 4, 4, L01)

questions.subject: Computer Organization
questions.text:
A 4 kilobyte (KB) byte-addressable memory is realized using four 1 KB memory blocks. Two input address lines (IA4 and IA3) are connected to the chip select (CS) port of these memory blocks through a decoder as shown in the figure. The remaining ten input address lines from IA11-IA0 are connected to the address port of these blocks. The chip select (CS) is active high.

The input memory addresses (IA11-IA0), in decimal, for the starting locations (Addr=0) of each block (indicated as X1, X2, X3, X4 in the figure) are among the options given below. Which one of the following options is CORRECT?
questions.solution:
The decoder inputs are IA4 and IA3, so bits 4 and 3 select the block; the other 10 lines address inside the block.

Starting location of each block (all other bits 0):
- X1: IA4 IA3 = 00 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] 0
- X2: 01 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] [latex]2^3=8[/latex]
- X3: 10 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] [latex]2^4=16[/latex]
- X4: 11 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] 16 + 8 = 24

Answer: (0, 8, 16, 24)

questions.subject: Digital Logic
questions.text:
Consider a sequential digital circuit consisting of T flip-flops and D flip-flops as shown in the figure. CLKIN is the clock input to the circuit. At the beginning, Q1, Q2 and Q3 have values 0, 1 and 1, respectively.

Which one of the given values of (Q1, Q2, Q3) can NEVER be obtained with this digital circuit?
questions.solution:
From the circuit: [latex]T_1=\overline{Q_3}[/latex], [latex]D_2=Q_1[/latex], [latex]T_3=Q_2[/latex].
Next state: [latex]Q_1^+=Q_1\oplus\overline{Q_3}[/latex], [latex]Q_2^+=Q_1[/latex], [latex]Q_3^+=Q_3\oplus Q_2[/latex].

Starting from (0, 1, 1):
011 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] 000 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] 100 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] 010 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] 101 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] 111 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] 110 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] 011 (repeats)

(0, 0, 1) never appears.

Answer: (0, 0, 1)

questions.subject: Digital Logic
questions.text:
A Boolean digital circuit is composed using two 4-input multiplexers (M1 and M2) and one 2-input multiplexer (M3) as shown in the figure. X0-X7 are the inputs of the multiplexers M1 and M2 and could be connected to either 0 or 1. The select lines of the multiplexers are connected to Boolean variables A, B and C as shown.

Which one of the following set of values of (X0, X1, X2, X3, X4, X5, X6, X7) will realise the Boolean function [latex] \bar{A}+\bar{A}\cdot \bar{C}+A\cdot \bar{B}\cdot C[/latex] ?
questions.solution:
M1 and M2 use selects (A, C), so input index = 2A + C. M3 picks M1 when B = 0 and M2 when B = 1.

Simplify: [latex]F=\bar A+\bar A\bar C+A\bar BC=\bar A+A\bar BC[/latex]

- B = 0 (M1): A = 0 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] F = 1 (X0 = X1 = 1); A = 1 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] F = C (X2 = 0, X3 = 1)
- B = 1 (M2): A = 0 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] F = 1 (X4 = X5 = 1); A = 1 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] F = 0 (X6 = X7 = 0)

Answer: (1, 1, 0, 1, 1, 1, 0, 0)

questions.subject: Digital Logic
questions.text:
Consider the IEEE-754 single precision floating point numbers P=0xC1800000 and Q=0x3F5C2EF4.
Which one of the following corresponds to the product of these numbers (i.e., P x Q), represented in the IEEE-754 single precision format?
questions.solution:
P = 0xC1800000: sign 1, exponent [latex]131\Rightarrow2^4[/latex], mantissa 0 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] [latex]P=-16[/latex].

Multiplying Q by [latex]-16[/latex] keeps Q's mantissa, makes the sign 1, and adds 4 to the exponent.
Q's exponent = 0x7E = 126 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] new exponent 130 = 1000 0010.

Bits: 1 | 1000 0010 | (Q's mantissa) [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] first 12 bits 1100 0001 0101 = C15, then the rest of the mantissa C2EF4.

Answer: 0xC15C2EF4

questions.subject: Data Structure
questions.text:
Let A be a priority queue for maintaining a set of elements. Suppose A is implemented using a max-heap data structure. The operation Extract-Max(A) extracts and deletes the maximum element from A. The operation Insert(A,key) inserts a new element key in A. The properties of a max-heap are preserved at the end of each of these operations.
When A contains n elements, which one of the following statements about the worst case running time of these two operations is TRUE?
options: Both Extract-Max(A) and Insert(A,key) run in O(1).
Both Extract-Max(A) and Insert(A,key) run in O(log(n)).
Extract-Max(A) runs in O(1) whereas Insert(A,key) runs in O(n).
Extract-Max(A) runs in O(1) whereas Insert(A,key) runs in O(log(n)).
questions.solution:
A heap of n elements has height about log n:
- Extract-Max: remove the root, move the last element to the root, and heapify down the height of the tree [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] [latex]O(\log n)[/latex].
- Insert: add at the end and bubble up to the root [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] [latex]O(\log n)[/latex].

Answer: Both run in O(log(n))

questions.subject: Data Structure
questions.solution:
foo returns the sum of a subtree and prints it after both children (post-order):
- node 3 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] prints 3
- node 8 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] prints 8
- node 5 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] 5 + 3 + 8 = 16
- node 13 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] 13
- node 11 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] 11 + 0 + 13 = 24
- root 10 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] 10 + 16 + 24 = 50

Answer: 3 8 16 13 24 50

questions.subject: Discrete Mathematics
questions.text:
Let U = {1, 2,...,n}, where n is a large positive integer greater than 1000. Let k be a positive integer less than n. Let A, B be subsets of U with |A| = |B| = k and [latex] A\cap B=\phi [/latex]. We say that a permutation of U separates A from B if one of the following is true.

- All members of A appear in the permutation before any of the members of B.
- All members of B appear in the permutation before any of the members of A.

How many permutations of U separate A from B?
questions.solution:
Count the permutations step by step:
- Choose the 2k positions that A [latex]\cup[/latex] B will occupy: [latex]\binom{n}{2k}[/latex]
- Arrange the other [latex]n-2k[/latex] elements in the rest: [latex](n-2k)![/latex]
- In the chosen positions, put all of A first and then B, or B first and then A: 2 ways
- Arrange A among its k places and B among its k places: [latex](k!)^2[/latex]

Total [latex]=2\binom{n}{2k}(n-2k)!(k!)^2[/latex]

Answer: [latex]2\binom{n}{2k}(n-2k)!(k!)^2[/latex]

questions.subject: Discrete Mathematics
questions.text:
Let [latex] f:A\rightarrow B[/latex] be an onto (or surjective) function, where [latex]A[/latex] and [latex]B[/latex] are nonempty sets. Define an equivalence relation [latex] \sim [/latex] on the set [latex]A[/latex] as
[latex] a_1\sim a_2 \text{ if } f(a_1)=f(a_2),[/latex]
where [latex] a_1, a_2 \in A[/latex] . Let [latex] \varepsilon =\{[x]:x \in A\}[/latex] be the set of all the equivalence classes under [latex] \sim [/latex]. Define a new mapping [latex] F: \varepsilon \rightarrow B[/latex] as
[latex]F([x]) = f(x),[/latex] for all the equivalence classes [latex][x][/latex] in [latex] \varepsilon[/latex]
Which of the following statements is/are TRUE?
options: F is an onto (or surjective) function.
F is a one-to-one (or injective) function.
questions.solution:
Check each property of F:
- Well-defined: if [x] = [y], then f(x) = f(y), so F gives the same value for every representative (option 1 FALSE).
- Onto: for any b in B, f is onto, so f(a) = b for some a, and F([a]) = b.
- One-to-one: F([x]) = F([y]) means f(x) = f(y), so [latex]x\sim y[/latex] and [x] = [y].
- Onto and one-to-one [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] bijective.

Answer: Options 2, 3 and 4

questions.subject: Computer Network
questions.text:
Suppose you are asked to design a new reliable byte-stream transport protocol like TCP. This protocol, named myTCP, runs over a 100 Mbps network with Round Trip Time of 150 milliseconds and the maximum segment lifetime of 2 minutes.
Which of the following is/are valid lengths of the Sequence Number field in the myTCP header?
questions.solution:
The sequence numbers must not wrap around within one MSL. Bytes sent in 2 minutes:
[latex]\frac{100\times10^6}{8}\times120=1.5\times10^9[/latex] bytes

[latex]2^{30}\approx1.07\times10^9[/latex] (too small), [latex]2^{31}\approx2.15\times10^9[/latex] (enough). So the field needs at least 31 bits.

32, 34 and 36 bits are valid; 30 bits is not.

Answer: 32 bits, 34 bits, 36 bits

questions.subject: Discrete Mathematics
questions.text:
Let [latex]X[/latex] be a set and [latex]2^X[/latex] denote the powerset of [latex]X[/latex].
Define a binary operation [latex] \Delta [/latex] on [latex]2^X[/latex] as follows:
[latex]A \Delta B=(A-B) \cup (B-A)[/latex]
Let [latex] H=(2^X,\Delta ) [/latex]. Which of the following statements about [latex]H[/latex] is/are correct?
options: Every element in [latex]H[/latex] has an inverse, but [latex]H[/latex] is NOT a group.
For every [latex]A \in 2^X[/latex], the inverse of [latex]A[/latex] is the complement of [latex]A[/latex].
For every [latex]A \in 2^X[/latex], the inverse of [latex]A[/latex] is [latex]A[/latex].
questions.solution:
Check the group properties of symmetric difference on [latex]2^X[/latex]:
- Closed: [latex]A\Delta B\subseteq X[/latex]
- Associative: yes (it behaves like XOR on membership)
- Identity: [latex]\phi[/latex], since [latex]A\Delta\phi=A[/latex]
- Inverse: [latex]A\Delta A=\phi[/latex], so every A is its own inverse (not its complement: [latex]A\Delta A^c=X[/latex])

Answer: H is a group; the inverse of A is A

questions.subject: Computer Network
questions.text:
Suppose in a web browser, you click on the www.gate-2023.in URL. The browser cache is empty. The IP address for this URL is not cached in your local host, so a DNS lookup is triggered (by the local DNS server deployed on your local host) over the 3-tier DNS hierarchy in an iterative mode. No resource records are cached anywhere across all DNS servers.
Let RTT denote the round trip time between your local host and DNS servers in the DNS hierarchy. The round trip time between the local host and the web server hosting www.gate-2023.in is also equal to RTT. The HTML file associated with the URL is small enough to have negligible transmission time and negligible rendering time by your web browser, which references 10 equally small objects on the same web server.
Which of the following statements is/are CORRECT about the minimum elapsed time between clicking on the URL and your browser fully rendering it?
options: 7 RTTs, in case of non-persistent HTTP with 5 parallel TCP connections.
5 RTTs, in case of persistent HTTP with pipelining.
9 RTTs, in case of non-persistent HTTP with 5 parallel TCP connections.
6 RTTs, in case of persistent HTTP with pipelining.
questions.solution:
DNS (iterative, 3 tiers: root, TLD, authoritative) = 3 RTT.

Non-persistent, 5 parallel connections: base HTML = TCP setup + request = 2 RTT. The 10 objects go in 2 batches of 5, each batch 2 RTT (new connection each) = 4 RTT.
Total = 3 + 2 + 4 = 9 RTT.

Persistent with pipelining: TCP setup 1 RTT + HTML 1 RTT + all 10 objects pipelined in 1 RTT.
Total = 3 + 1 + 1 + 1 = 6 RTT.

Answer: 9 RTTs (non-persistent, 5 parallel) and 6 RTTs (persistent with pipelining)

questions.subject: Discrete Mathematics
questions.text:
Consider a random experiment where two fair coins are tossed. Let A be the event
that denotes HEAD on both the throws, B be the event that denotes HEAD on
the first throw, and C be the event that denotes HEAD on the second throw.
Which of the following statements is/are TRUE?
questions.solution:
[latex]P(A)=\frac14,\ P(B)=P(C)=\frac12[/latex].

- A and B: [latex]P(A\cap B)=P(A)=\frac14\ne P(A)P(B)=\frac18[/latex] [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] not independent (same for A and C).
- B and C: [latex]P(B\cap C)=\frac14=\frac12\cdot\frac12[/latex] [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] independent.
- So [latex]P(B|C)=P(B)[/latex] [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE.

Answer: B and C are independent; Prob(B|C) = Prob(B)

questions.subject: Algorithm
questions.text:
Consider functions Function 1 and Function 2 expressed in pseudocode as follows:

Let [latex]f_1(n)[/latex] and [latex]f_2(n)[/latex] denote the number of times the statement [latex]"x = x + 1"[/latex] is executed in Function 1 and Function 2, respectively.
Which of the following statements is/are TRUE?
questions.solution:
Count how many times x = x + 1 runs in each function:
- Function 1: the inner loop runs n, then n/2, n/4, [latex]\ldots[/latex] times: [latex]f_1(n)\approx n+\frac n2+\frac n4+\cdots\lt2n[/latex] [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] [latex]\Theta(n)[/latex].
- Function 2: [latex]f_2(n)=100n[/latex] [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] [latex]\Theta(n)[/latex].

Both are linear: [latex]f_1\in\Theta(f_2)[/latex] and [latex]f_1\in O(n)[/latex]. They are not strictly smaller or larger than each other, so o and [latex]\omega[/latex] fail.

Answer: [latex]f_1(n)\in\Theta(f_2(n))[/latex] and [latex]f_1(n)\in O(n)[/latex]

questions.subject: Discrete Mathematics
questions.text:
Let [latex]G[/latex] be a simple, finite, undirected graph with vertex set [latex] \{v_1,...,v_n\}[/latex]. Let [latex] \Delta (G)[/latex] denote the maximum degree of [latex]G[/latex] and let [latex] N=\{1,2,...\} [/latex] denote the set of all possible colors. Color the vertices of [latex]G[/latex] using the following greedy strategy: for [latex]i = 1,...,n[/latex]
[latex]color(v_i)\leftarrow min\{ j \in N: \text{ no neighbour of } v_i \text{ is colored } j\}[/latex]
Which of the following statements is/are TRUE?
options: This procedure results in a proper vertex coloring of [latex]G[/latex].
The number of colors used is at most [latex] \Delta (G)+1[/latex].
The number of colors used is at most[latex] \Delta (G)[/latex].
The number of colors used is equal to the chromatic number of [latex]G[/latex].
questions.solution:
Checking each statement:
- Each vertex gets the smallest colour not used by any neighbour, so no edge joins equal colours [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] proper colouring [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE.
- A vertex has at most [latex]\Delta(G)[/latex] neighbours, so among colours [latex]1\ldots\Delta+1[/latex] one is always free [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] at most [latex]\Delta(G)+1[/latex] colours [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE.
- [latex]K_n[/latex] needs n = [latex]\Delta+1[/latex] colours, so "at most [latex]\Delta(G)[/latex]" is FALSE.
- A bad vertex order can use more colours than the chromatic number (e.g. on some bipartite graphs) [latex]\text{---}[/latex] FALSE.

Answer: Options 1 and 2

questions.subject: Algorithm
questions.text:
Let [latex]U = \{1, 2, 3\}[/latex]. Let [latex]2^U[/latex] denote the powerset of [latex]U[/latex]. Consider an undirected graph [latex]G[/latex] whose vertex set is [latex]2^U[/latex]. For any [latex]A,B \in 2^U, (A,B)[/latex] is an edge in [latex]G[/latex] if and only if (i) [latex]A \neq B[/latex], and (ii) either [latex]A \subseteq B[/latex] or [latex]B \subseteq A[/latex]. For any vertex [latex]A[/latex] in [latex]G[/latex], the set of all possible orderings in which the vertices of [latex]G[/latex] can be visited in a Breadth First Search (BFS) starting from [latex]A[/latex] is denoted by [latex]B(A)[/latex].
If [latex]\phi [/latex] denotes the empty set, then the cardinality of [latex]B(\phi ) [/latex] is ____.
questions.solution:
[latex]\phi[/latex] is a subset of every set, so [latex]\phi[/latex] is adjacent to all the other [latex]2^3-1=7[/latex] vertices.

BFS from [latex]\phi[/latex] visits all 7 neighbours at level 1, and these 7 can be visited in any order: [latex]7!=5040[/latex].

Answer: 5040

questions.subject: Operating System
questions.text:
Consider the following two-dimensional array D in the C programming language, which is stored in row-major order:

int D[128][128];

Demand paging is used for allocating memory and each physical page frame holds 512 elements of the array D. The Least Recently Used (LRU) page-replacement policy is used by the operating system. A total of 30 physical page frames are allocated to a process which executes the following code snippet:

for (int i = 0; i < 128; i++)
       for (int j = 0; j < 128; j++) 
                   D[j][i] *= 10;

The number of page faults generated during the execution of this code snippet is _____.
questions.solution:
One page = 512 ints = 4 rows of D (each row has 128 ints). D has 128 rows [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] 32 pages.

The loop accesses D[j][i] column-wise: for each i, j goes 0 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] 127, touching all 32 pages in order (one page per 4 rows).

With 30 frames and LRU, cycling through 32 pages means each page is evicted before it is needed again. So every new page in each pass faults: 32 faults per value of i.

Total [latex]=128\times32=4096[/latex]

Answer: 4096

questions.subject: Operating System
questions.text:
Consider a computer system with 57-bit virtual addressing using multi-level tree-structured page tables with L levels for virtual to physical address translation. The page size is 4 KB (1 KB = 1024 B) and a page table entry at any of the levels occupies 8 bytes.
The value of L is ______.
questions.solution:
Page size 4 KB [latex]=2^{12}[/latex] [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] 12 offset bits. VPN bits [latex]=57-12=45[/latex].

One page-table page holds [latex]\frac{4096}{8}=512=2^9[/latex] entries [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] each level resolves 9 bits.

Levels [latex]L=\frac{45}{9}=5[/latex]

Answer: 5

questions.subject: Data Structure
questions.text:
Consider a sequence [latex]a[/latex] of elements [latex]a_0 = 1, a_1 = 5, a_2 = 7, a_3 = 8, a_4 = 9, \; and \; a_5 = 2[/latex]. The following operations are performed on a stack [latex]S[/latex] and a queue [latex]Q[/latex], both of which are initially empty.

I: push the elements of a from [latex]a_0[/latex] to [latex]a_5[/latex] in that order into [latex]S[/latex].
II: enqueue the elements of a from [latex]a_0[/latex] to [latex]a_5[/latex] in that order into [latex]Q[/latex].
III: pop an element from [latex]S[/latex].
IV: dequeue an element from [latex]Q[/latex].
V: pop an element from [latex]S[/latex].
VI: dequeue an element from [latex]Q[/latex].
VII: dequeue an element from [latex]Q[/latex] and push the same element into [latex]S[/latex].
VIII: Repeat operation VII three times.
IX: pop an element from [latex]S[/latex].
X: pop an element from [latex]S[/latex].

The top element of [latex]S[/latex] after executing the above operations is ___.
questions.solution:
After I and II: S = [1, 5, 7, 8, 9, 2] (top = 2), Q = [1, 5, 7, 8, 9, 2] (front = 1).
- III: pop S [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] removes 2
- IV: dequeue Q [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] removes 1
- V: pop S [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] removes 9 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] S = [1, 5, 7, 8]
- VI: dequeue Q [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] removes 5 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] Q = [7, 8, 9, 2]
- VII + VIII (4 times): move 7, 8, 9, 2 from Q to S [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] S = [1, 5, 7, 8, 7, 8, 9, 2]
- IX, X: pop 2 and 9 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] top = 8

Answer: 8

questions.subject: Compiler Design
questions.text:
Consider the syntax directed translation given by the following grammar and semantic rules. Here [latex]N, I, F \; and \; B[/latex] are non-terminals. [latex]N[/latex] is the starting non-terminal, and [latex]\#,0 \; and \; 1[/latex] are lexical tokens corresponding to input letters [latex]"\#","0" \; and \; "1"[/latex], respectively. [latex]X.val[/latex] denotes the synthesized attribute (a numeric value) associated with a non-terminal [latex]X[/latex]. [latex]I_1[/latex] and [latex]F_1[/latex] denote occurrences of [latex]I[/latex] and [latex]F[/latex] on the right hand side of a production, respectively. For the tokens [latex]0[/latex] and [latex]1[/latex], [latex]0.val=0[/latex] and [latex]1.val=1[/latex].

The value computed by the translation scheme for the input string
[latex]\begin{aligned} N & \rightarrow I \# F & N.val=I.val+F.val \\ I &\rightarrow I_1B & I.val = (2 I1.val) + B.val\\ I &\rightarrow B&I.val = B.val\\ F &\rightarrow BF_1& F.val = \frac{1}{2}(B.val + F1.val)\\ F &\rightarrow B& F.val = \frac{1}{2} B.val\\ B&\rightarrow 0& B.val = 0.val\\ B &\rightarrow 1&B.val = 1.val \end{aligned} [/latex]
[latex]10\# 011[/latex]

is ____ (Rounded off to three decimal places)
questions.solution:
Integer part "10" (binary):
I for "1" = 1; I for "10" = [latex]2\times1+0=2[/latex].

Fraction part "011" (evaluated right to left):
- F("1") = [latex]\frac12\times1=0.5[/latex]
- F("11") = [latex]\frac12(1+0.5)=0.75[/latex]
- F("011") = [latex]\frac12(0+0.75)=0.375[/latex]

N.val = 2 + 0.375 = 2.375 (i.e. binary 10.011).

Answer: 2.375

questions.subject: Database Management System
questions.text:
Consider the following table named Student in a relational database. The primary key of this table is rollNum.
[latex]\begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|} \hline \\ rollNum&name&gender&marks \\ \hline 1&Naman&M&62\\ \hline 2&Aliya&F&70 \\ \hline 3&Aliya &F&80 \\ \hline 4&James&M&82\\ \hline 5&Swati&F&65\\ \hline \end{array} [/latex]
The SQL query below is executed on this database.

SELECT *
FROM Student
WHERE gender = 'F' AND
 marks > 65;

The number of rows returned by the query is ______
questions.solution:
Rows with gender = 'F' and marks [latex]\gt[/latex] 65:
- Aliya, 70 True
- Aliya, 80 True
- Swati, 65 False (65 is not greater than 65)

SELECT * returns full rows, so the duplicate name does not matter.

Answer: 2

questions.subject: Database Management System
questions.text:
Consider a database of fixed-length records, stored as an ordered file. The database has 25,000 records, with each record being 100 bytes, of which the primary key occupies 15 bytes. The data file is block-aligned in that each data record is fully contained within a block. The database is indexed by a primary index file, which is also stored as a block-aligned ordered file. The figure below depicts this indexing scheme.

Suppose the block size of the file system is 1024 bytes, and a pointer to a block occupies 5 bytes. The system uses binary search on the index file to search for a record with a given key. You may assume that a binary search on an index file of [latex]b[/latex] blocks takes [latex]\left \lceil \log_2 b \right \rceil [/latex] block accesses in the worst case.
Given a key, the number of block accesses required to identify the block in the data file that may contain a record with the key, in the worst case, is _____
questions.solution:
Compute the index size step by step:
- Records per data block = [latex]\lfloor1024/100\rfloor=10[/latex] [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] data blocks = 25000 / 10 = 2500.
- Primary (sparse) index has one entry per data block: 2500 entries of [latex]15+5=20[/latex] bytes.
- Entries per index block = [latex]\lfloor1024/20\rfloor=51[/latex] [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] index blocks = [latex]\lceil2500/51\rceil=50[/latex].

Binary search on the index: [latex]\lceil\log_2 50\rceil=6[/latex] block accesses identify the data block.

Answer: 6

questions.subject: Theory of Computation
questions.text:
Consider the language L over the alphabet {0, 1}, given below:

[latex]L = \{w \in \{0, 1\}^* | w \text{ does not contain three or more consecutive 1's} \}.[/latex]
The minimum number of states in a Deterministic Finite-State Automaton (DFA) for L is _____.
questions.solution:
The DFA only needs to remember how many 1s have just been seen in a row:
- q0: last symbol 0 (or start)
- q1: one 1
- q2: two 1s
- q3: three 1s seen [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] dead (non-final) state

q0, q1, q2 are final. A 0 returns q0/q1/q2 to q0. All 4 states are distinguishable.

Answer: 4

questions.subject: Computer Organization
questions.text:
An 8-way set associative cache of size 64 KB (1 KB = 1024 bytes) is used in a system with 32-bit address. The address is sub-divided into TAG, INDEX, and BLOCK OFFSET.
The number of bits in the TAG is ____.
questions.solution:
Size of one way [latex]=\frac{64\text{ KB}}{8}=8\text{ KB}=2^{13}[/latex] bytes.

INDEX + OFFSET bits together address one way, so they total 13 bits (the block size does not matter).

TAG [latex]=32-13=19[/latex] bits

Answer: 19

questions.subject: Computer Network
questions.text:
The forwarding table of a router is shown below.
[latex]\begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|} \hline \\ Subnet \; Number&Subnet \;Mask&Interface ID \\ \hline 200.150.0.0 &255.255.0.0& 1\\ \hline 200.150.64.0 &255.255.224.0 &2\\ \hline 200.150.68.0 &255.255.255.0 &3\\ \hline 200.150.68.64 &255.255.255.224 &4 \\ \hline Default & &0\\ \hline \end{array} [/latex]
A packet addressed to a destination address 200.150.68.118 arrives at the router. It will be forwarded to the interface with ID _____.
questions.solution:
Check each entry for 200.150.68.118 (longest prefix wins):
- 200.150.0.0/16 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] matches
- 200.150.64.0/19 (third octet 64-95) [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] 68 matches
- 200.150.68.0/24 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] matches
- 200.150.68.64/27 (last octet 64-95) [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] 118 does not match

Longest match is /24 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] interface 3.

Answer: 3

questions.subject: General Aptitude
questions.text: We reached the station late, and _______ missed the train.
questions.solution:
"Nearly missed the train" means almost missed it (but caught it). Near is not an adverb here, and "utterly / mostly missed" do not make sense.

Answer: nearly

questions.subject: General Aptitude
questions.text:
Kind : _______ : : Often : Frequently
(By word meaning)
questions.solution:
Often and frequently are synonyms. As a noun, kind means sort or type, so kind : type is the matching synonym pair.

Answer: Type

questions.subject: General Aptitude
questions.text:
A series of natural numbers [latex]F_1,F_2,F_3,F_4,F_5,F_6,F_7,... [/latex] obeys [latex]F_{n+1}=F_n+F_{n-1} [/latex] for all integers [latex]n \geq 2[/latex].
If [latex]F_6=37[/latex], and [latex]F_7=60[/latex], then what is [latex]F_1[/latex]?
questions.solution:
Work backwards using [latex]F_{n-1}=F_{n+1}-F_n[/latex]:
- [latex]F_5=60-37=23[/latex]
- [latex]F_4=37-23=14[/latex]
- [latex]F_3=23-14=9[/latex]
- [latex]F_2=14-9=5[/latex]
- [latex]F_1=9-5=4[/latex]

Answer: 4

questions.subject: General Aptitude
questions.text:
A survey for a certain year found that 90% of pregnant women received medical care at least once before giving birth. Of these women, 60% received medical care from doctors, while 40% received medical care from other healthcare providers.
Given this information, which one of the following statements can be inferred with certainty?
options:
More than half of the pregnant women received medical care at least once from a
doctor.

Less than half of the pregnant women received medical care at least once from a
doctor.

More than half of the pregnant women received medical care at most once from a
doctor.

Less than half of the pregnant women received medical care at most once from a
doctor.
questions.solution:
Women who received care from doctors = 60% of 90% = 54% of all pregnant women.

54% is more than half, so more than half received care at least once from a doctor. The data says nothing about "at most once".

Answer: More than half of the pregnant women received medical care at least once from a doctor

questions.subject: General Aptitude
questions.text:
Looking at the surface of a smooth 3-dimensional object from the outside, which
one of the following options is TRUE?
options: The surface of the object must be concave everywhere.
The surface of the object must be convex everywhere.
The surface of the object may be concave in some places and convex in other places.
The object can have edges, but no corners.
questions.solution:
A smooth 3D object (e.g. a peanut or a bowl-shaped surface) can bulge outward in some places and curve inward in others. Nothing forces it to be convex or concave everywhere, and "smooth" rules out edges.

Answer: The surface may be concave in some places and convex in other places

questions.subject: General Aptitude
questions.text:
The country of Zombieland is in distress since more than 75% of its working population is suffering from serious health issues. Studies conducted by competent health experts concluded that a complete lack of physical exercise among its working population was one of the leading causes of their health issues. As one of the measures to address the problem, the Government of Zombieland has decided to provide monetary incentives to those who ride bicycles to work.
Based only on the information provided above, which one of the following statements can be logically inferred with certainty?
options: All the working population of Zombieland will henceforth ride bicycles to work.

Riding bicycles will ensure that all of the working population of Zombieland is free
of health issues.

The health experts suggested to the Government of Zombieland to declare riding
bicycles as mandatory.

The Government of Zombieland believes that riding bicycles is a form of physical
exercise.
questions.solution:
The government gives incentives for cycling because lack of exercise is a cause of the health issues. This only makes sense if it believes cycling is a form of physical exercise.

The other options claim things the passage does not support (everyone will cycle, all will be healthy, experts asked for it to be mandatory).

Answer: The Government of Zombieland believes that riding bicycles is a form of physical exercise

questions.subject: General Aptitude
questions.text:
Consider two functions of time [latex](t)[/latex],
[latex]f(t)=0.01t^2[/latex]
[latex]g(t)=4t[/latex]
where
[latex]0 \lt t \lt \infty[/latex]
Now consider the following two statements:

(i) For some [latex] t \gt 0, g(t) \gt f(t)[/latex].
(ii) There exists a [latex]T[/latex], such that [latex]f(t) \gt g(t)[/latex] for all [latex]t \gt T[/latex] .

Which one of the following options is TRUE?
questions.solution:
[latex]g(t) \gt f(t)\iff4t \gt 0.01t^2\iff t \lt 400[/latex] (for t [latex]\gt[/latex] 0).

- (i) For any t between 0 and 400, g(t) [latex]\gt[/latex] f(t) [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] correct.
- (ii) Take T = 400: for all t [latex]\gt[/latex] 400, f(t) [latex]\gt[/latex] g(t) [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] correct.

Answer: both (i) and (ii) are correct

questions.subject: General Aptitude
questions.text:
Which one of the following sentence sequences creates a coherent narrative?

(i) Once on the terrace, on her way to her small room in the corner, she notices the man right away.
(ii) She begins to pant by the time she has climbed all the stairs.
(iii) Mina has bought vegetables and rice at the market, so her bags are heavy.
(iv) He was leaning against the parapet, watching the traffic below.
questions.solution:
Follow the story:
- (iii) introduces Mina and her heavy bags.
- (ii) explains that she pants after climbing the stairs (because of the bags).
- (i) she reaches the terrace and notices "the man".
- (iv) describes him ("He was leaning[latex]\ldots[/latex]").

Answer: (iii), (ii), (i), (iv)

questions.subject: General Aptitude
questions.text:
[latex]f(x)[/latex] and [latex]g(y)[/latex] are functions of [latex]x[/latex] and [latex]y[/latex], respectively, and
 [latex]f(x)=g(y)[/latex] for all real
values of [latex]x[/latex] and [latex]y[/latex]. Which one of the following options is necessarily TRUE for all
 [latex]x[/latex] and [latex]y[/latex]?
questions.solution:
Fix y = [latex]y_0[/latex]: then [latex]f(x)=g(y_0)[/latex] for every x, so f is constant. In the same way g is constant, and the two constants are equal.

They need not be 0, and option 4 would force [latex]g(y)=0[/latex].

Answer: f(x) = g(y) = constant

questions.subject: General Aptitude
questions.text: Which one of the options best describes the transformation of the 2-dimensional figure P to Q, and then to R, as shown?
options:
Operation 1: A clockwise rotation by [latex]90^{\circ} [/latex] about an axis perpendicular to the plane of the figure
Operation 2: A reflection along a horizontal line

Operation 1: A counter clockwise rotation by [latex]90^{\circ} [/latex] about an axis perpendicular to the plane of the figure
Operation 2: A reflection along a horizontal line

Operation 1: A clockwise rotation by [latex]90^{\circ} [/latex] about an axis perpendicular to the plane of the figure
Operation 2: A reflection along a vertical line

Operation 1: A counter clockwise rotation by [latex]180^{\circ} [/latex] about an axis perpendicular to the plane of the figure
Operation 2: A reflection along a vertical line
questions.solution:
Track the long spike of the star:
- P [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] Q: the spike turns from pointing right to pointing down [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] a 90[latex]^\circ[/latex] clockwise rotation.
- Q [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] R: the spike flips from pointing down to pointing up, with left and right unchanged [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] reflection along a horizontal line.

Answer: Clockwise rotation by 90[latex]^\circ[/latex], then reflection along a horizontal line

questions.subject: Discrete Mathematics
questions.text: Let [latex]f: \mathbb{R} \rightarrow \mathbb{R} [/latex] be a function such that [latex]f(x)=\max \left\{x, x^3\right\}, x \in \mathbb{R} [/latex], where [latex]\mathbb{R} [/latex] is the set of all real numbers. The set of all points where [latex]f(x) [/latex] is NOT differentiable is
questions.solution:
Compare [latex]x[/latex] and [latex]x^3[/latex]: they are equal at [latex]x=-1,0,1[/latex]. So [latex]f(x)=x[/latex] for [latex]x\le -1[/latex], [latex]x^3[/latex] on [latex][-1,0][/latex], [latex]x[/latex] on [latex][0,1][/latex], [latex]x^3[/latex] for [latex]x\ge1[/latex].

At every switching point the two pieces have different slopes ([latex]\frac{d}{dx}x=1[/latex], [latex]\frac{d}{dx}x^3=3x^2[/latex]):
- [latex]x=-1[/latex]: slopes [latex]1[/latex] and [latex]3[/latex] [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] corner
- [latex]x=0[/latex]: slopes [latex]0[/latex] and [latex]1[/latex] [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] corner
- [latex]x=1[/latex]: slopes [latex]1[/latex] and [latex]3[/latex] [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] corner

Everywhere else [latex]f[/latex] is a polynomial, hence differentiable.

Answer: [latex]\{-1,0,1\}[/latex]

questions.subject: Engineering Mathematics
questions.text:
The product of all eigenvalues of the matrix [latex]\begin{bmatrix}
1 & 2 & 3\\ 
4 & 5 &6 \\ 
7 &8  & 9
\end{bmatrix}[/latex] is
questions.solution:
Product of all eigenvalues [latex]=\det(A)[/latex].

[latex]\det(A)=1(45-48)-2(36-42)+3(32-35)=-3+12-9=0[/latex]

(Quick check: [latex]R_1+R_3=2R_2[/latex], so the rows are dependent and the matrix is singular.)

Answer: 0

questions.subject: Digital Logic
questions.text: Consider a system that uses 5 bits for representing signed integers in 2's complement format. In this system, two integers [latex]A [/latex] and [latex]B [/latex] are represented as [latex]A=01010 [/latex] and [latex]B=11010 [/latex]. Which one of the following operations will result in either an arithmetic overflow or an arithmetic underflow?
questions.solution:
With 5-bit 2's complement the range is [latex]-16[/latex] to [latex]+15[/latex].

[latex]A=01010=+10[/latex], [latex]B=11010=-6[/latex].

- [latex]A+B=4[/latex] [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] fits
- [latex]A-B=10+6=16[/latex] [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] exceeds +15, overflow
- [latex]B-A=-16[/latex] [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] fits (lowest value)
- [latex]2B=-12[/latex] [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] fits

Answer: A [latex]-[/latex] B

questions.subject: Discrete Mathematics
questions.text: Consider a permutation sampled uniformly at random from the set of all permutations of [latex]\{1,2,3, \cdots, n\} [/latex] for some [latex]n \geq 4 [/latex]. Let [latex]X [/latex] be the event that 1 occurs before 2 in the permutation, and [latex]Y [/latex] the event that 3 occurs before 4 . Which one of the following statements is TRUE?
options: The events [latex]X [/latex] and [latex]Y [/latex] are mutually exclusive
Event [latex]X [/latex] is more likely than event [latex]Y [/latex]
questions.solution:
By symmetry, 1 is before 2 in half of all permutations, so [latex]P(X)=\frac12[/latex]; similarly [latex]P(Y)=\frac12[/latex].

The relative order of {1,2} and the relative order of {3,4} involve different elements, and all 4 combinations (12/21 with 34/43) are equally likely, so [latex]P(X\cap Y)=\frac14=P(X)P(Y)[/latex] [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] independent.

- Not mutually exclusive: 1 2 3 4 [latex]\ldots[/latex] satisfies both.
- Neither must occur: 2 1 4 3 [latex]\ldots[/latex] satisfies none.
- Equally likely, so X is not more likely than Y.

Answer: X and Y are independent

questions.subject: Computer Organization
questions.text: Which one of the following statements is FALSE?
options:
In the cycle stealing mode of DMA, one word of data is transferred between an I/O
device and main memory in a stolen cycle

For bulk data transfer, the burst mode of DMA has a higher throughput than the
cycle stealing mode

Programmed I/O mechanism has a better CPU utilization than the interrupt driven
I/O mechanism

The CPU can start executing an interrupt service routine faster with vectored
interrupts than with non-vectored interrupts
questions.solution:
Checking each statement:
- Cycle stealing: DMA takes one bus cycle and moves one word [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE.
- Burst mode keeps the bus for the whole block (no repeated bus requests), so it has higher throughput for bulk transfer [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE.
- Programmed I/O has better CPU utilization than interrupt-driven I/O [latex]\text{---}[/latex] FALSE. In programmed I/O the CPU keeps polling the device status and wastes cycles; interrupt-driven I/O lets the CPU do other work until the device interrupts.
- Vectored interrupts give the ISR address directly (no polling to find the device), so ISR starts faster [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE.

Answer: Programmed I/O has better CPU utilization than interrupt driven I/O (FALSE)

questions.subject: Computer Network
questions.text:
A user starts browsing a webpage hosted at a remote server. The browser opens a single TCP connection to fetch the entire webpage from the server. The webpage consists of a top-level index page with multiple embedded image objects. Assume that all caches (e.g., DNS cache, browser cache) are all initially empty. The following packets leave the user's computer in some order.

(i) HTTP GET request for the index page
(ii) DNS request to resolve the web server's name to its IP address
(iii) HTTP GET request for an image object
(iv) TCP SYN to open a connection to the web server

Which one of the following is the CORRECT chronological order (earliest in time to latest) of the packets leaving the computer ?
questions.solution:
Order in which the packets leave the computer:
1. (ii) DNS request [latex]\text{---}[/latex] the IP address of the server is needed before anything else (caches are empty).
2. (iv) TCP SYN [latex]\text{---}[/latex] open the TCP connection with the server.
3. (i) GET index page [latex]\text{---}[/latex] first request on the connection.
4. (iii) GET image [latex]\text{---}[/latex] the browser knows about the image only after it receives and parses the index page.

Answer: (ii), (iv), (i), (iii)

questions.subject: Algorithm
questions.text:
Given an integer array of size [latex]N[/latex], we want to check if the array is sorted (in either
ascending or descending order). An algorithm solves this problem by making a
single pass through the array and comparing each element of the array only with its
adjacent elements. The worst-case time complexity of this algorithm is
questions.solution:
The algorithm compares each pair of adjacent elements once: [latex]N-1[/latex] comparisons in the worst case (when the array is actually sorted, it must check every pair before saying YES).

It cannot do less: any element not examined could break the order. So the worst case is [latex]\Theta(N)[/latex], i.e. both [latex]O(N)[/latex] and [latex]\Omega(N)[/latex].

Answer: both [latex]O(N)[/latex] and [latex]\Omega(N)[/latex]

questions.subject: C Programming
options: The program gets stuck in an infinite loop
questions.solution:
Integer division is used.

Iteration 1: [latex]a=6/12+1=0+1=1[/latex], then [latex]a=a+b=1+0=1[/latex].
Iteration 2: [latex]a=1/12+1=0+1=1[/latex] again, and so on.

[latex]a[/latex] is stuck at 1, so the condition [latex]a \lt 10[/latex] is always true and printf is never reached.

Answer: The program gets stuck in an infinite loop

questions.subject: C Programming
options: The program will terminate with no outpu
The program will terminate with 4321 as output
The program will terminate with 1234 as output
questions.solution:
Each call of fX() reads one character and, if it is not newline, calls fX() again before printing. Each call has its own local [latex]a[/latex].

Calls read: '1' [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] '2' [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] '3' [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] '4' [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] '\n'. The last call reads newline, makes no further call and prints nothing.

While returning, the calls print their characters in reverse order: 4, 3, 2, 1. Then main returns normally.

Answer: The program will terminate with 4321 as output

questions.subject: Database Management System
questions.text: Let S be the specification: "Instructors teach courses. Students register for courses. Courses are allocated classrooms. Instructors guide students." Which one of the following ER diagrams CORRECTLY represents S?
questions.solution:
From the specification we need 4 entity sets [latex]\text{---}[/latex] Instructor, Course, Student, Classroom [latex]\text{---}[/latex] and 4 relationships:
Instructor-Teaches-Course, Student-Registers-Course, Course-Allocated-Classroom, Instructor-Guides-Student.

- (i): Registration is drawn as an entity and Student as a relationship [latex]\text{---}[/latex] wrong.
- (ii): no Student entity; an extra Projects entity is used [latex]\text{---}[/latex] wrong.
- (iii): Classroom is attached directly to Course and the Allocation relationship does not connect Classroom [latex]\text{---}[/latex] wrong.
- (iv): all four entities and all four relationships are connected correctly.

Answer: (iv)

questions.subject: Data Structure
questions.text:
In a B+ tree, the requirement of at least half-full (50%) node occupancy is relaxed
for which one of the following cases?
questions.solution:
In a B+ tree of order [latex]m[/latex], every node (internal or leaf) must be at least half full [latex]\text{---}[/latex] except the root.

The root can have as few as 2 children (or just 1 key if it is a leaf), otherwise a small tree could never be built.

Answer: Only the root node

questions.subject: Database Management System
questions.text:
Which of the following statements about a relation R in first normal form (1NF)
is/are TRUE ?
options: R can have a multi-attribute key
R cannot have a foreign key
R cannot have a composite attribute
R cannot have more than one candidate key
questions.solution:
1NF only requires every attribute value to be atomic (no multi-valued or composite attributes).

- R can have a multi-attribute key [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE (e.g. key (roll_no, course_id)). This is about keys, not about values.
- R cannot have a foreign key [latex]\text{---}[/latex] FALSE, 1NF puts no restriction on foreign keys.
- R cannot have a composite attribute [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE, a composite attribute is non-atomic and must be split into simple attributes.
- R cannot have more than one candidate key [latex]\text{---}[/latex] FALSE.

Answer: R can have a multi-attribute key; R cannot have a composite attribute

questions.subject: Theory of Computation
questions.text: Let [latex]L_1, L_2 [/latex] be two regular languages and [latex]L_3 [/latex] a language which is not regular. Which of the following statements is/are always TRUE?
questions.solution:
Checking each statement:
- [latex]L_1\cap\overline{L_2}=\phi[/latex] only means [latex]L_1\subseteq L_2[/latex]. Equality also needs [latex]L_2\subseteq L_1[/latex] [latex]\text{---}[/latex] FALSE.
- [latex]L_1\cup L_3[/latex] can be regular: take [latex]L_1=\Sigma^*[/latex], then [latex]L_1\cup L_3=\Sigma^*[/latex] [latex]\text{---}[/latex] FALSE (not always).
- If [latex]\overline{L_3}[/latex] were regular, then its complement [latex]L_3[/latex] would be regular (closure under complement). So [latex]\overline{L_3}[/latex] is not regular [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE.
- Regular languages are closed under complement and union, so [latex]\overline{L_1}\cup\overline{L_2}[/latex] is regular [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE.

Answer: [latex]\overline{L_3}[/latex] is not regular; [latex]\overline{L_1}\cup\overline{L_2}[/latex] is regular

questions.subject: Operating System
questions.text: Which of the following statements about threads is/are TRUE?
options: Threads can only be implemented in kernel space
Each thread has its own file descriptor table for open files
All the threads belonging to a process share a common stack
Threads belonging to a process are by default not protected from each other
questions.solution:
Checking each statement:
- Threads can also be implemented in user space (user-level threads) [latex]\text{---}[/latex] FALSE.
- The file descriptor table belongs to the process and is shared by all its threads [latex]\text{---}[/latex] FALSE.
- Every thread has its own stack (and registers, PC) [latex]\text{---}[/latex] FALSE.
- Threads share the same address space, so one thread can read/overwrite another thread's data; there is no protection between them [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE.

Answer: Threads belonging to a process are by default not protected from each other

questions.subject: Operating System
questions.text: Which of the following process state transitions is/are NOT possible?
questions.solution:
Checking each statement:
- Running [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] Ready: possible (preemption / time slice over).
- Waiting [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] Running: NOT possible. When the I/O finishes, the process goes to Ready; only the scheduler can move it to Running.
- Ready [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] Waiting: NOT possible. A process can block (request I/O) only while it is running.
- Running [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] Terminated: possible (exit).

Answer: Waiting to Running, Ready to Waiting

questions.subject: Compiler Design
questions.text: Which of the following is/are Bottom-Up Parser(s)?
questions.solution:
Bottom-up parsers build the parse tree from the leaves up to the root using reductions: shift-reduce parsers, operator precedence parser and the LR family (LR(0), SLR, LALR, CLR).

Predictive parser and LL(1) parser are top-down parsers.

Answer: Shift-reduce Parser, LR Parser

questions.subject: Discrete Mathematics
questions.text: Let [latex]A [/latex] and [latex]B [/latex] be two events in a probability space with [latex]P(A)=0.3, P(B)=0.5 [/latex], and [latex]P(A \cap B)=0.1 [/latex]. Which of the following statements is/are TRUE?
options: The two events [latex]A [/latex] and [latex]B [/latex] are independent
[latex]P\left(A \cap B^c\right)=0.2 [/latex], where [latex]B^c [/latex] is the complement of the event [latex]B [/latex]
[latex]P\left(A^c \cap B^c\right)=0.4 [/latex], where [latex]A^c [/latex] and [latex]B^c [/latex] are the complements of the events [latex]A [/latex] and [latex]B [/latex], respectively
questions.solution:
Checking each statement:
- Independence: [latex]P(A)P(B)=0.15\ne0.1[/latex] [latex]\text{---}[/latex] FALSE.
- [latex]P(A\cup B)=0.3+0.5-0.1=0.7[/latex] [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE.
- [latex]P(A\cap B^c)=P(A)-P(A\cap B)=0.3-0.1=0.2[/latex] [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE.
- [latex]P(A^c\cap B^c)=1-P(A\cup B)=0.3\ne0.4[/latex] [latex]\text{---}[/latex] FALSE.

Answer: [latex]P(A\cup B)=0.7[/latex] and [latex]P(A\cap B^c)=0.2[/latex]

questions.subject: Digital Logic
questions.text: Consider the circuit shown below where the gates may have propagation delays. Assume that all signal transitions occur instantaneously and that wires have no delays. Which of the following statements about the circuit is/are CORRECT?
options: With no propagation delays, the output Y is always logic Zero
With no propagation delays, the output Y is always logic One

With propagation delays, the output Y can have a transient logic One after X
transitions from logic Zero to logic One

With propagation delays, the output Y can have a transient logic Zero after X
transitions from logic One to logic Zero
questions.solution:
The circuit computes [latex]Y=X\cdot\overline{X}[/latex].

- No delays: [latex]X\cdot\overline{X}=0[/latex] always [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] Y is always 0 (option 1 TRUE, option 2 FALSE).
- X goes 0 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] 1: the AND gate sees X = 1 immediately, but the NOT output is still 1 until its delay passes. For that short time both inputs are 1, so Y gives a transient 1 (glitch) [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE.
- X goes 1 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] 0: the direct input becomes 0 immediately, so Y stays 0 no matter what the NOT output does [latex]\text{---}[/latex] no transient, FALSE.

Answer: Y is always 0 with no delays; with delays Y can have a transient 1 after X goes 0 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] 1

questions.subject: Computer Network
questions.text: TCP client P successfully establishes a connection to TCP server [latex]\mathrm{Q} [/latex]. Let [latex]N_P [/latex] denote the sequence number in the SYN sent from [latex]\mathrm{P} [/latex] to [latex]\mathrm{Q} [/latex]. Let [latex]N_Q [/latex] denote the acknowledgement number in the SYN ACK from Q to P. Which of the following statements is/are CORRECT?
options: The sequence number [latex]N_P [/latex] is chosen randomly by [latex]\mathrm{P} [/latex]
The sequence number [latex]N_P [/latex] is always 0 for a new connection
The acknowledgement number [latex]N_Q [/latex] is equal to [latex]N_P [/latex]
The acknowledgement number [latex]N_Q [/latex] is equal to [latex]N_P+1 [/latex]
questions.solution:
Checking each statement:
- The initial sequence number (ISN) is chosen randomly (to avoid confusion with old segments and for security) [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE; it is not always 0.
- A SYN segment consumes one sequence number, so Q acknowledges with the next expected number: [latex]N_Q=N_P+1[/latex] [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE (so [latex]N_Q=N_P[/latex] is false).

Answer: [latex]N_P[/latex] is chosen randomly by P; [latex]N_Q=N_P+1[/latex]

questions.subject: Computer Organization
questions.text: Consider a 5-stage pipelined processor with Instruction Fetch (IF), Instruction Decode (ID), Execute (EX), Memory Access (MEM), and Register Writeback (WB) stages. Which of the following statements about forwarding is/are CORRECT?
options:
In a pipelined execution, forwarding means the result from a source stage of an
earlier instruction is passed on to the destination stage of a later instruction

In forwarding, data from the output of the MEM stage can be passed on to the
input of the EX stage of the next instruction
Forwarding cannot prevent all pipeline stalls

Forwarding does not require any extra hardware to retrieve the data from the
pipeline stages
questions.solution:
Checking each statement:
- Option 1: this is exactly the definition of forwarding (bypassing) [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE.
- Option 2: a value available at the output of MEM (e.g. a loaded value) can be fed to the EX input of a later instruction [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE.
- Option 3: forwarding cannot remove every stall. Example: load followed immediately by an instruction using the loaded value still needs 1 stall (load-use hazard) [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE.
- Option 4: forwarding needs extra hardware (extra paths, multiplexers, hazard detection logic) [latex]\text{---}[/latex] FALSE.

Answer: Options 1, 2 and 3

questions.subject: Computer Network
questions.text:
Which of the following fields is/are modified in the IP header of a packet going out
of a network address translation (NAT) device from an internal network to an
external network?
questions.solution:
For an outgoing packet, NAT replaces the private source IP (and port) with its public IP.

Because a header field changed, the header checksum must be recomputed.

Destination IP is unchanged (it is the outside server), and total length is unchanged (payload size is the same).

Answer: Source IP, Header Checksum

questions.subject: Discrete Mathematics
questions.text: Let [latex]A [/latex] and [latex]B [/latex] be non-empty finite sets such that there exist one-to-one and onto functions (i) from [latex]A [/latex] to [latex]B [/latex] and (ii) from [latex]A \times A [/latex] to [latex]A \cup B [/latex]. The number of possible values of [latex]|A| [/latex] is ___
questions.solution:
Bijection [latex]A\to B[/latex] [latex]\Rightarrow[/latex] [latex]|A|=|B|=n[/latex].
Bijection [latex]A\times A\to A\cup B[/latex] [latex]\Rightarrow[/latex] [latex]n^2=|A\cup B|[/latex].

But [latex]n\le|A\cup B|\le 2n[/latex], so [latex]n\le n^2\le 2n[/latex] [latex]\Rightarrow[/latex] [latex]n\le2[/latex].

- [latex]n=1[/latex]: [latex]A=B[/latex], [latex]|A\cup B|=1=1^2[/latex] True
- [latex]n=2[/latex]: take A and B disjoint, [latex]|A\cup B|=4=2^2[/latex] True

So [latex]|A|\in\{1,2\}[/latex].

Answer: 2

questions.subject: Data Structure
questions.text:
Consider the operator precedence and associativity rules for the integer arithmetic operators given in the table below.
[latex]\begin{array}{|c|l|l|} \hline Operator & Precedence & Associativity \\ \hline+ & Highest & Left \\ \hline- & High & Right \\ \hline* & Medium & Right \\ \hline / & Low & Right \\ \hline \end{array} [/latex]
The value of the expression [latex]3+1+5 * 2 / 7+2-4-7-6 / 2 [/latex] as per the above rules is _____
questions.solution:
Precedence: + (highest) [latex]\gt[/latex] [latex]-[/latex] [latex]\gt[/latex] * [latex]\gt[/latex] / (lowest). The lowest-precedence operator is applied last, so / splits the expression:
[latex](3+1+5*2)\;/\;(7+2-4-7-6)\;/\;2[/latex]

First part: + binds before *, so [latex](3+1+5)*2=9*2=18[/latex].
Second part: + first: [latex]7+2=9[/latex]. Then [latex]-[/latex] is right associative: [latex]9-(4-(7-6))=9-(4-1)=6[/latex].

/ is right associative: [latex]18/(6/2)=18/3=6[/latex].

Answer: 6

questions.subject: Algorithm
questions.text:
The number of spanning trees in a complete graph of 4 vertices labelled A, B, C,
and D is _________
questions.solution:
Number of spanning trees of a complete graph [latex]K_n[/latex] (Cayley's formula) [latex]=n^{n-2}[/latex].

[latex]4^{4-2}=16[/latex]

Answer: 16

questions.subject: Database Management System
questions.text:
Consider the following two relations, [latex]R(A, B) [/latex] and [latex]S(A, C) [/latex] :
[latex]\boldsymbol{R} \begin{array}{|c|c|} \hline \boldsymbol{A} & \boldsymbol{B} \\ \hline 10 & 20 \\ \hline 20 & 30 \\ \hline 30 & 40 \\ \hline 30 & 50 \\ \hline 50 & 95 \\ \hline \end{array}[/latex]


[latex]\boldsymbol{S} \begin{array}{|c|c|} \hline \boldsymbol{A} & \boldsymbol{C} \\ \hline 10 & 90 \\ \hline 30 & 45 \\ \hline 40 & 80 \\ \hline \end{array} [/latex]
The total number of tuples obtained by evaluating the following expression [latex] \sigma_{B \lt C}\left(R \bowtie_{R . A=S . A} S\right) [/latex] is ____
questions.solution:
Join on [latex]R.A=S.A[/latex]:
- A = 10: (10, 20, 90) [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] [latex]20 \lt 90[/latex] True
- A = 30: (30, 40, 45) [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] [latex]40 \lt 45[/latex] True
- A = 30: (30, 50, 45) [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] [latex]50 \lt 45[/latex] False
(A = 20, 50 in R and A = 40 in S have no match.)

Answer: 2

questions.subject: Computer Network
questions.text:
Consider a network path [latex]\mathrm{P}-\mathrm{Q}-\mathrm{R} [/latex] between nodes [latex]\mathrm{P} [/latex] and [latex]\mathrm{R} [/latex] via router [latex]\mathrm{Q} [/latex]. Node [latex]\mathrm{P} [/latex] sends a file of size [latex]10^6 [/latex] bytes to [latex]R [/latex] via this path by splitting the file into chunks of [latex]10^3 [/latex] bytes each. Node [latex]P [/latex] sends these chunks one after the other without any wait time between the successive chunk transmissions. Assume that the size of extra headers added to these chunks is negligible, and that the chunk size is less than the MTU.
Each of the links [latex]\mathrm{P}-\mathrm{Q} [/latex] and [latex]\mathrm{Q}-\mathrm{R} [/latex] has a bandwidth of [latex]10^6 \mathrm{bits} / \mathrm{sec} [/latex], and negligible propagation latency. Router [latex]Q [/latex] immediately transmits every packet it receives from [latex]P [/latex] to [latex]R [/latex], with negligible processing and queueing delays. Router [latex]Q [/latex] can simultaneously receive on link [latex]P-Q [/latex] and transmit on [latex]\operatorname{link} Q-R [/latex].
Assume P starts transmitting the chunks at time [latex]t=0 [/latex]. Which one of the following options gives the time (in seconds, rounded off to 3 decimal places) at which [latex]\mathrm{R} [/latex] receives all the chunks of the file?
questions.solution:
Number of chunks [latex]=10^6/10^3=1000[/latex]. Each chunk [latex]=8000[/latex] bits, so transmission time on a link [latex]=\frac{8000}{10^6}=8[/latex] ms.

P sends the chunks back to back: the last chunk is fully sent by P at [latex]1000\times8\text{ ms}=8[/latex] s.
Q forwards each chunk while receiving the next, so only the last chunk adds one more transmission of 8 ms on Q-R.

Total [latex]=8+0.008=8.008[/latex] s.

Answer: 8.008

questions.subject: Compiler Design
questions.text:
Consider the following syntax-directed definition (SDD).

[latex] \begin{array}{|l|l|} \hline S \rightarrow DHTU & \{ S.val = D.val + H.val + T.val + U.val; \} \\ \hline D \rightarrow "M"D_1 & \{ D.val =5+D_1 . val; \} \\ \hline D \rightarrow \epsilon & \{ D.val =-5 ;\} \\ \hline H \rightarrow "L" H_1 & \{ H.val =5 * 10+H_1 . val; \} \\ \hline H \rightarrow \epsilon & \{ H.val =-10 ;\} \\ \hline T \rightarrow "C" T_1 & \{T . v a l=5 * 100+T_1 . val; \} \\ \hline T \rightarrow \epsilon & \{T . v a l=-5 ;\} \\ \hline U \rightarrow "K" & \{ U.val =5 ;\} \\ \hline \end{array} [/latex]

Given "MMLK" as the input, which one of the following options is the CORRECT value computed by the SDD (in the attribute S.val)?
questions.solution:
Input "MMLK" [latex]\Rightarrow[/latex] D = "MM", H = "L", T = [latex]\epsilon[/latex], U = "K".

- [latex]D[/latex]: [latex]5+5+(-5)=5[/latex]
- [latex]H[/latex]: [latex]5*10+(-10)=40[/latex]
- [latex]T=\epsilon[/latex]: [latex]-5[/latex]
- [latex]U[/latex]: [latex]5[/latex]

[latex]S.val=5+40-5+5=45[/latex]

Answer: 45

questions.subject: Compiler Design
questions.text:
Consider the following grammar [latex]G [/latex], with [latex]S [/latex] as the start symbol. The grammar [latex]G [/latex] has three incomplete productions denoted by (1), (2), and (3).

[latex] \begin{aligned} & S \rightarrow d a T \mid \quad(1) \\ & T \rightarrow a S|b T|(2) \\ & R \rightarrow \text { (3) } \mid \epsilon \end{aligned} [/latex]

The set of terminals is [latex]\{a, b, c, d, f\} [/latex]. The FIRST and FOLLOW sets of the different non-terminals are as follows.

[latex] \begin{aligned} & \operatorname{FIRST}(S)=\{c, d, f\}, \operatorname{FIRST}(T)=\{a, b, \epsilon\}, \operatorname{FIRST}(R)=\{c, \epsilon\} \\ & \operatorname{FOLLOW}(S)=\operatorname{FOLLOW}(T)=\{c, f, \$\}, \operatorname{FOLLOW}(R)=\{f\} \end{aligned} [/latex]

Which one of the following options CORRECTLY fills in the incomplete productions?
options:
(1) [latex]S \rightarrow f R [/latex]
(2) [latex]T \rightarrow c T [/latex]
(3) [latex]R \rightarrow c R [/latex]

(1) [latex]S \rightarrow R f [/latex]
(2) [latex]T \rightarrow c T [/latex]
(3) [latex]R \rightarrow c R [/latex]
questions.solution:
Use the given FIRST and FOLLOW sets:
- [latex]FIRST(S)=\{c,d,f\}[/latex] but [latex]daT[/latex] gives only d, so (1) must give c and f. [latex]S\rightarrow Rf[/latex] gives [latex](FIRST(R)-\epsilon)\cup\{f\}=\{c,f\}[/latex] True ([latex]S\rightarrow fR[/latex] gives only f).
- [latex]\epsilon\in FIRST(T)[/latex], so (2) is [latex]T\rightarrow\epsilon[/latex].
- [latex]FIRST(R)=\{c,\epsilon\}[/latex], so (3) starts with c.

Check FOLLOW with [latex]R\rightarrow cTR[/latex]: [latex]FOLLOW(T)\supseteq FIRST(R)-\epsilon=\{c\}[/latex] and [latex]FOLLOW(R)=\{f\}[/latex] (from [latex]S\rightarrow Rf[/latex]); together with $ this gives [latex]FOLLOW(S)=FOLLOW(T)=\{c,f,\$\}[/latex] True. With [latex]R\rightarrow cR[/latex], c could never follow T.

Answer: (1) [latex]S\rightarrow Rf[/latex] (2) [latex]T\rightarrow\epsilon[/latex] (3) [latex]R\rightarrow cTR[/latex]

questions.subject: Compiler Design
questions.text:
Consider the following pseudo-code.
[latex] \begin{array}{ll} L 1: & t 1=-1 \\ L 2: & t 2=0 \\ L 3: & t 3=0 \\ L 4: & t 4=4 * t 3 \\ L 5: & t 5=4 * t 2 \\ L 6: & t 6=t 5 * M \\ L 7: & t 7=t 4+t 6 \\ L 8: & t 8=a[t 7] \\ L 9: & if \; t 8 \lt = max \; goto \; L 11 \\ L 10: & t 1=t 8 \\ L 11: & t 3=t 3+1 \\ L 12: & if \; t 3 \lt M \; goto L 4 \\ L 13: & t 2=t 2+1 \\ L 14: & if \; t 2 \lt N \; goto \; L 3 \\ L 15: & max =t 1 \end{array} [/latex]
Which of of the following options CORRECTLY specifies the number of basic blocks and the number of instructions in the largest basic block, respectively?
questions.solution:
Leaders: first instruction (L1), targets of jumps (L3, L4, L11) and instructions right after a conditional jump (L10, L13, L15).

Basic blocks:
- B1: L1-L2 (2)
- B2: L3 (1)
- B3: L4-L9 (6)
- B4: L10 (1)
- B5: L11-L12 (2)
- B6: L13-L14 (2)
- B7: L15 (1)

7 basic blocks; the largest (B3) has 6 instructions.

Answer: 7 and 6

questions.subject: Operating System
questions.solution:
Final a depends only on which a-update runs first; final b only on which b-update runs first.
- a: [latex](1+1)\times2=4[/latex] if T1's update is first, [latex]2\times1+1=3[/latex] otherwise.
- b: [latex](1+1)\times2=4[/latex] if T1's update is first, [latex]3[/latex] otherwise.

- T1 then T2: (4, 4). T2 then T1: (3, 3).
- T1: a=a+1, T2: b=2b, T2: a=2a, T1: b=b+1 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] (4, 3).
- (3, 4) is impossible: it needs T2's a-update before T1's a-update and T1's b-update before T2's b-update. But in program order T1 does a before b and T2 does b before a, so this creates a cycle.

Answer: (a=4, b=4); (a=3, b=3); (a=4, b=3)

questions.subject: Data Structure
questions.text: An array [latex][82,101,90,11,111,75,33,131,44,93] [/latex] is heapified. Which one of the following options represents the first three elements in the heapified array?
questions.solution:
Build a max-heap bottom-up (heapify from index [latex]\lfloor10/2\rfloor=5[/latex] down to 1):
[82, 101, 90, 11, 111, 75, 33, 131, 44, 93]

- i=5 (111): child 93 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] no change.
- i=4 (11): children 131, 44 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] swap with 131.
- i=3 (90): children 75, 33 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] no change.
- i=2 (101): children 131, 111 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] swap with 131 (101 then fine above 11, 44).
- i=1 (82): swap with 131, then with 111, then with 93.

Heap: [131, 111, 90, 101, 93, 75, 33, 11, 44, 82]

Answer: 131, 111, 90

questions.subject: Algorithm
questions.text:
Consider the following recurrence relation:
[latex] T(n)=\left\{\begin{array}{c} \sqrt{n} T(\sqrt{n})+n \text { for } n \geq 1, \\ 1 \quad \text { for } n=1 . \end{array}\right. [/latex]
Which one of the following options is CORRECT?
questions.solution:
Divide both sides by [latex]n[/latex]: [latex]\frac{T(n)}{n}=\frac{T(\sqrt n)}{\sqrt n}+1[/latex].

Let [latex]S(n)=\frac{T(n)}{n}[/latex]. Then [latex]S(n)=S(\sqrt n)+1[/latex].

Taking square roots repeatedly, [latex]n\to n^{1/2}\to n^{1/4}\to\cdots[/latex] reaches a constant after [latex]\log\log n[/latex] steps, adding 1 each step. So [latex]S(n)=\Theta(\log\log n)[/latex].

[latex]T(n)=n\,S(n)=\Theta(n\log\log n)[/latex]

Answer: [latex]T(n)=\Theta(n\log\log n)[/latex]

questions.subject: Data Structure
questions.text: Consider a binary min-heap containing 105 distinct elements. Let [latex]k[/latex]  be the index (in the underlying array) of the maximum element stored in the heap. The number of possible values of [latex]k[/latex] is
questions.solution:
In a min-heap every parent is smaller than its children, so the maximum element cannot have a child [latex]\text{---}[/latex] it must be a leaf. Any leaf can hold it.

In an array heap of [latex]n[/latex] elements, leaves are at indices [latex]\lfloor n/2\rfloor+1[/latex] to [latex]n[/latex].

[latex]n=105[/latex]: leaves are 53 to 105 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] [latex]105-52=53[/latex] positions.

Answer: 53

questions.subject: Database Management System
questions.text: The symbol [latex] \rightarrow [/latex] indicates functional dependency in the context of a relational database. Which of the following options is/are TRUE?
options: [latex] ((X, Y) \rightarrow Z \text { and } W \rightarrow Y) \text { implies }(X, W) \rightarrow Z  [/latex]
[latex] (X \rightarrow Y \text { and } Y \rightarrow Z) \text { implies } X \rightarrow Z [/latex]
questions.solution:
Checking each statement:
- [latex](X,Y)\rightarrow(Z,W)[/latex] does not give [latex]X\rightarrow(Z,W)[/latex]; Y may be required [latex]\text{---}[/latex] FALSE.
- Decomposition rule: [latex]XY\rightarrow ZW[/latex] [latex]\Rightarrow[/latex] [latex]XY\rightarrow Z[/latex] [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE.
- Pseudo-transitivity: [latex]W\rightarrow Y[/latex] [latex]\Rightarrow[/latex] [latex]XW\rightarrow XY[/latex] (augment by X), and [latex]XY\rightarrow Z[/latex], so [latex]XW\rightarrow Z[/latex] [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE.
- Transitivity: [latex]X\rightarrow Y,\;Y\rightarrow Z[/latex] [latex]\Rightarrow[/latex] [latex]X\rightarrow Z[/latex] [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE.

Answer: Options 2, 3 and 4

questions.subject: Discrete Mathematics
questions.text: Let [latex] G [/latex] be a directed graph and [latex] T [/latex] a depth first search (DFS) spanning tree in [latex] G [/latex] that is rooted at a vertex [latex] v [/latex]. Suppose [latex] T [/latex] is also a breadth first search (BFS) tree in [latex] G [/latex], rooted at [latex] v [/latex]. Which of the following statements is/are TRUE for every such graph [latex] G [/latex] and tree [latex] T [/latex] ?
options: There are no back-edges in [latex] G [/latex] with respect to the tree [latex] T [/latex]
There are no cross-edges in [latex] G [/latex] with respect to the tree [latex] T [/latex]
There are no forward-edges in [latex] G [/latex] with respect to the tree [latex] T [/latex]
The only edges in [latex] G [/latex] are the edges in [latex] T [/latex]
questions.solution:
In a BFS tree, every edge [latex]u\rightarrow w[/latex] of G satisfies [latex]level(w)\le level(u)+1[/latex].

A forward edge goes from [latex]u[/latex] to a non-child descendant [latex]w[/latex], so [latex]level(w)\ge level(u)+2[/latex] [latex]\text{---}[/latex] this contradicts BFS. Hence there are no forward edges [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE.

The others can fail:
- Back edge: G = {v[latex]\rightarrow[/latex]a, a[latex]\rightarrow[/latex]v}. Tree {v[latex]\rightarrow[/latex]a} is both DFS and BFS tree; a[latex]\rightarrow[/latex]v is a back edge.
- Cross edge: G = {v[latex]\rightarrow[/latex]a, v[latex]\rightarrow[/latex]b, b[latex]\rightarrow[/latex]a}. DFS visits a then b; b[latex]\rightarrow[/latex]a is a cross edge, and the tree is also the BFS tree.
- So G can also have edges outside T.

Answer: There are no forward-edges in G with respect to T

questions.subject: Database Management System
questions.text:
Consider the following read-write schedule [latex] S [/latex] over three transactions [latex] T_1, T_2 [/latex], and [latex] T_3 [/latex], where the subscripts in the schedule indicate transaction IDs:

[latex] S: r_1(z) ; w_1(z) ; r_2(x) ; r_3(y) ; w_3(y) ; r_2(y) ; w_2(x) ; w_2(y) ; [/latex]

Which of the following transaction schedules is/are conflict equivalent to [latex] S [/latex] ?
questions.solution:
Conflicting pairs (same item, different transactions, at least one write):
- z: only T1 uses it [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] T1 has no conflict with anyone.
- x: only T2 uses it.
- y: [latex]r_3(y),w_3(y)[/latex] come before [latex]r_2(y),w_2(y)[/latex] [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] T3 must come before T2.

So any serial order with T3 before T2 is conflict equivalent, and T1 can be anywhere: [latex]T_1T_3T_2,\;T_3T_2T_1,\;T_3T_1T_2[/latex].
[latex]T_1T_2T_3[/latex] puts T2 before T3 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] not equivalent.

Answer: [latex]T_1T_3T_2[/latex], [latex]T_3T_2T_1[/latex], [latex]T_3T_1T_2[/latex]

questions.subject: Digital Logic
questions.text:
Consider a Boolean expression given by [latex] F(X, Y, Z)=\Sigma(3,5,6,7) [/latex].
Which of the following statements is/are CORRECT?
options: [latex] F(X, Y, Z) [/latex] is independent of input [latex] Y [/latex]
[latex] F(X, Y, Z) [/latex] is independent of input [latex] X [/latex]
questions.solution:
Minterms 3, 5, 6, 7 = 011, 101, 110, 111 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] F = 1 when at least two inputs are 1 (majority function).

- Maxterms are the remaining combinations: [latex]\Pi(0,1,2,4)[/latex] [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE.
- Majority function [latex]=XY+YZ+XZ[/latex] [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE.
- Depends on Y: [latex]F(1,0,0)=0[/latex] but [latex]F(1,1,0)=1[/latex] [latex]\text{---}[/latex] so not independent of Y.
- Depends on X: [latex]F(0,1,0)=0[/latex] but [latex]F(1,1,0)=1[/latex] [latex]\text{---}[/latex] so not independent of X.

Answer: [latex]F=\Pi(0,1,2,4)[/latex] and [latex]F=XY+YZ+XZ[/latex]

questions.subject: C Programming
options: If the inputs are [latex] x=20, y=10 [/latex], then the return value is greater than [latex] 2^{20} [/latex]
If the inputs are [latex] x=20, y=20 [/latex], then the return value is greater than [latex] 2^{20} [/latex]
If the inputs are [latex] x=20, y=10 [/latex], then the return value is less than [latex] 2^{10} [/latex]
If the inputs are [latex] x=10, y=20 [/latex], then the return value is greater than [latex] 2^{20} [/latex]
questions.solution:
Each iteration does [latex]x\leftarrow2x+y[/latex], repeated [latex]y[/latex] times. Solving:
[latex]f(x,y)=2^y x+(2^y-1)y=2^y(x+y)-y[/latex]

- [latex]x=20,y=10[/latex]: [latex]1024\times30-10=30710[/latex]. This is less than [latex]2^{20}[/latex] but more than [latex]2^{10}[/latex] [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] options 1 and 3 FALSE.
- [latex]x=20,y=20[/latex]: [latex]2^{20}\times40-20 \gt 2^{20}[/latex] [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] TRUE.
- [latex]x=10,y=20[/latex]: [latex]2^{20}\times30-20 \gt 2^{20}[/latex] [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] TRUE.
(Both values are about [latex]4\times10^7[/latex], so no int overflow.)

Answer: Options 2 and 4

questions.subject: Engineering Mathematics
questions.text: Let [latex] A [/latex] be any [latex] n \times m [/latex] matrix, where [latex] m > n [/latex]. Which of the following statements is/are TRUE about the system of linear equations [latex] A x=0 [/latex] ?
options: There exist at least [latex] m-n [/latex] linearly independent solutions to this system
There exist [latex] m-n [/latex] linearly independent vectors such that every solution is a linear combination of these vectors
There exists a non-zero solution in which at least [latex] m-n [/latex] variables are 0
There exists a solution in which at least [latex] n [/latex] variables are non-zero
questions.solution:
[latex]rank(A)\le n \lt m[/latex], so the solution space has dimension [latex]m-rank(A)\ge m-n[/latex].

- At least [latex]m-n[/latex] linearly independent solutions [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE.
- "[latex]m-n[/latex] vectors span every solution" fails when the dimension is larger, e.g. A = zero matrix (dimension m) [latex]\text{---}[/latex] FALSE.
- [latex]A=[1\;\;1][/latex] ([latex]n=1,m=2[/latex]): solutions are [latex]t(1,-1)[/latex]; no non-zero solution has a zero entry, though [latex]m-n=1[/latex] [latex]\text{---}[/latex] FALSE.
- [latex]A=\begin{bmatrix}1&0&0\\0&1&0\end{bmatrix}[/latex]: solutions [latex](0,0,t)[/latex] have only 1 non-zero variable [latex]\lt n=2[/latex] [latex]\text{---}[/latex] FALSE.

Answer: There exist at least [latex]m-n[/latex] linearly independent solutions

questions.subject: Theory of Computation
questions.text:
Consider the 5 -state DFA [latex] M [/latex] accepting the language [latex] L(M) \subset(0+1)^* [/latex] shown below. For any string [latex] w \in(0+1)^* [/latex] let [latex] n_0(w) [/latex] be the number of [latex] 0^{\prime} s [/latex] in [latex] w [/latex] and [latex] n_1(w) [/latex] be the number of 1 's in [latex] w [/latex].

Which of the following statements is/are FALSE?
options: States 2 and 4 are distinguishable in [latex] M [/latex]
States 3 and 4 are distinguishable in [latex] M [/latex]
States 2 and 5 are distinguishable in [latex] M [/latex]
Any string [latex] w [/latex] with [latex] n_0(w)=n_1(w) [/latex] is in [latex] L(M) [/latex]
questions.solution:
Reading 0 moves 1[latex]\rightarrow[/latex]2[latex]\rightarrow[/latex]3[latex]\rightarrow[/latex]1, reading 1 moves 1[latex]\rightarrow[/latex]4[latex]\rightarrow[/latex]5[latex]\rightarrow[/latex]1, and the reverse arrows undo a step. So the DFA tracks [latex](n_0-n_1)\bmod 3[/latex]:
state 1 = 0, states 2 and 5 = 1, states 3 and 4 = 2.

[latex]L(M)=\{w: n_0(w)\equiv n_1(w)\pmod 3\}[/latex], and states with the same value are equivalent.

- 2 and 4 (values 1 and 2): distinguishable (input "1": 2[latex]\rightarrow[/latex]1 accept, 4[latex]\rightarrow[/latex]5 reject) [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE.
- 3 and 4: both value 2 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] equivalent [latex]\text{---}[/latex] statement FALSE.
- 2 and 5: both value 1 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] equivalent [latex]\text{---}[/latex] statement FALSE.
- [latex]n_0=n_1[/latex] [latex]\Rightarrow[/latex] difference 0 [latex]\Rightarrow[/latex] accepted [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE.

Answer: "States 3 and 4 are distinguishable" and "States 2 and 5 are distinguishable"

questions.subject: Discrete Mathematics
questions.text: The chromatic number of a graph is the minimum number of colours used in a proper colouring of the graph. Let [latex] G [/latex] be any graph with [latex] n [/latex] vertices and chromatic number [latex] k [/latex]. Which of the following statements is/are always TRUE?
options: [latex]G[/latex] contains a complete subgraph with [latex]k[/latex] vertices
[latex]G[/latex] contains an independent set of size at least [latex]n/k[/latex]
[latex]G[/latex] contains a vertex of degree at least [latex]k[/latex]
questions.solution:
Checking each statement:
- Complete subgraph of size k: FALSE. The 5-cycle [latex]C_5[/latex] has [latex]\chi=3[/latex] but no triangle.
- Independent set of size [latex]\ge n/k[/latex]: TRUE. The k colour classes are independent sets covering n vertices, so the largest has at least [latex]n/k[/latex] vertices.
- At least [latex]k(k-1)/2[/latex] edges: TRUE. In a minimum colouring, every pair of colour classes must have an edge between them (otherwise merge the two classes and use [latex]k-1[/latex] colours). That gives [latex]\binom{k}{2}[/latex] edges.
- Vertex of degree [latex]\ge k[/latex]: FALSE. [latex]K_k[/latex] has [latex]\chi=k[/latex] but every degree is [latex]k-1[/latex].

Answer: Options 2 and 3

questions.subject: Discrete Mathematics
questions.text: Consider the operators [latex] \diamond [/latex] and [latex] \square [/latex] defined by [latex] a \diamond b=a+2 b, a \square b=a b [/latex], for positive integers. Which of the following statements is/are TRUE?
options: Operator [latex] \diamond [/latex] over the operator [latex] \square [/latex] obeys the distributive law
Operator [latex] \square [/latex] over the operator [latex] \diamond [/latex] obeys the distributive law
questions.solution:
Checking each statement:
- [latex]\diamond[/latex] associative? [latex](a\diamond b)\diamond c=a+2b+2c[/latex], [latex]a\diamond(b\diamond c)=a+2b+4c[/latex] [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] NO.
- [latex]\square[/latex] is ordinary multiplication [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] associative, YES.
- [latex]\diamond[/latex] over [latex]\square[/latex]: [latex]a\diamond(b\square c)=a+2bc[/latex], but [latex](a\diamond b)\square(a\diamond c)=(a+2b)(a+2c)[/latex]. For [latex]a=b=c=1[/latex]: 3 vs 9 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] NO.
- [latex]\square[/latex] over [latex]\diamond[/latex]: [latex]a\square(b\diamond c)=a(b+2c)=ab+2ac=(a\square b)\diamond(a\square c)[/latex] [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] YES.

Answer: [latex]\square[/latex] is associative; [latex]\square[/latex] distributes over [latex]\diamond[/latex]

questions.subject: Computer Organization
questions.text:
Consider two set-associative cache memory architectures: WBC, which uses the
write back policy, and WTC, which uses the write through policy. Both of them use
the LRU (Least Recently Used) block replacement policy. The cache memory is
connected to the main memory. Which of the following statements is/are TRUE?
options: A read miss in WBC never evicts a dirty block

A read miss in WTC never triggers a write back operation of a cache block to
main memory
A write hit in WBC can modify the value of the dirty bit of a cache block

A write miss in WTC always writes the victim cache block to main memory
before loading the missed block to the cache
questions.solution:
Checking each statement:
- WBC read miss: the LRU victim may be dirty and then it must be written back [latex]\text{---}[/latex] FALSE ("never" is wrong).
